AWS Lambda now supports a 30-minute function timeout for Event Functions that run on demand, doubling the 15-minute limit for synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping (ESM) invocations. On Lambda Managed Instances, synchronous invocations also support up to 30 minutes, while asynchronous and ESM invocations keep the 90-minute timeout rolled out in September 2026. You can now run long-running workloads such as AI inference, media transcoding, and financial calculations for spiky or steady-state traffic without re-architecting your applications.

Recent findings suggest that customers use Event Functions to build event-driven processors, API backends, and data pipelines. By default, Event Functions run on demand, and Lambda scales them automatically to handle spiky traffic. For steady-state traffic, you can also run them on Lambda Managed Instances, which runs functions on Amazon EC2 instances and maintains the operational simplicity of Lambda. For data-intensive workloads such as AI inference and media processing that run on demand and need longer continuous execution, the 15-minute function timeout had required customers to adopt architectural workarounds. With today's launch, these workloads can run for up to 30 minutes, including when you use Lambda durable functions or invoke your functions from AWS Step Functions Standard workflows.

Industry observers note that for Event Functions that run on demand, the 30-minute timeout is available in all commercial AWS Regions. On Lambda Managed Instances, it is available for synchronous invocations in all Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. You can set the function timeout by using the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. You can also use coding assistants such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex with the Agent Toolkit for AWS. Standard AWS Lambda pricing applies. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide.

arXiv:2508.05022v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a framework for dependent default times where each name defaults when an increasing driver crosses an independent unit exponential threshold. As in Gueye and Jeanblanc (2022), the drivers may jump, so defaults may occur at stopping times of the reference filtration, including predictable ones, and a common jump may cause no, one or several simultaneous defaults. For general drivers, we derive the conditional joint survival law by a backward recursion; it is an explicit product of survival functions if and only if, for every set of names, the predictable reduction of the compensator of their first default time is deterministic. If, moreover, defaults avoid predictable stopping times, the law is a fatal shock law with hazards identified from the drivers; predictable default atoms can rule this out. Examples include L\'evy subordinators and, with random reductions but explicit laws, Liu's model and shot-noise drivers with memory.

#14325. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3789 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • Sources indicate that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Sources indicate that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) indicated that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

Recent findings suggest that we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

According to recent reports, for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

According to recent reports, RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Industry observers note that each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

It has been revealed that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

It has been revealed that A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

It has been revealed that each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

It has been revealed that of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

Recent findings suggest that this example reveals how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

It has been revealed that the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

It has been revealed that each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

The figure below highlights how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

According to recent reports, to obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which indicated that 0.1 worked best).

Recent findings suggest that we performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

In a recent development, before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

It has been revealed that we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

Recent findings suggest that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

In a recent development, we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

In a recent development, we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each enhancement below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own revision. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

It has been revealed that "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

In a recent development, despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

According to recent reports, the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

Recent findings suggest that during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets latest tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

Sources indicate that we ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

In a recent development, this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

Today, AWS confirms deal-level revenue attribution for AWS Revenue Measurement (previously Partner Revenue Measurement) capabilities. AWS Partners can now see how the AWS revenue measured for their products maps to specific AWS Marketplace offers and/or APN Customer Engagements (ACE) opportunities. Until now, partners who implemented AWS Revenue Measurement via Resource Tagging, User Agent String or AWS Marketplace Metering could view aggregated, product-level attributed revenue. With this launch, partners can view attributed revenue by offers and opportunities on the Attributed Revenue dashboard in AWS Partner Central for components hosted in partners' own AWS accounts. Two fresh capabilities make this possible: Revenue Attribution IDs and Marketplace Revenue Share.

In a recent development, A Revenue Attribution ID is a unique identifier that allows partners to allocate a product's measured AWS revenue to specific offers and opportunities. Partners create a Revenue Attribution ID, associate it with their deals, and enter a monthly attributed revenue allocation percentage for each deal. Partners with SaaS products on AWS Marketplace can automate allocation to offers with Marketplace Revenue Share. Each month, partners enter the percentage of the product's attributed revenue contributed by AWS Marketplace deals in the Revenue Attribution page, and AWS then calculates the attributed revenue for each active offer. Partners can use Revenue Attribution IDs alongside Marketplace Revenue Share to adjust a calculated offer amount or attribute revenue to opportunities for future months. Both capabilities build on AWS Revenue Measurement, so partners can extend their current product-level implementations to gain deal-level insights.

Recent findings suggest that partners can manage Revenue Attribution IDs and Marketplace Revenue Share in AWS Partner Central or through the AWS Revenue Measurement and Marketplace Revenue Share APIs. AWS Revenue Measurement is generally available in all commercial Regions. To learn more, review the onboarding guide.

Here’s what’s happening and why the ParkMobile data beach settlement is raising eyebrows online.

Also: Hackers stole 1 billion records from Salesforce customer databases with this simple trick – don’t fall for it.

Sources indicate that in 2021, hackers accessed sensitive data from more than 21 million ParkMobile customers, including license plate numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, and mailing addresses. The hackers didn’t get any payment information.

Recent findings suggest that parkMobile denied any wrongdoing but agreed to a settlement to avoid the cost and time of going to court. If you filed a claim, you could choose to get your payment in cash — up to $25. If you didn’t file a claim but you were still affected, you probably received an email this week with your alternative payment — $1.

“As part of the agreed resolution,” the email explained, “you are entitled to receive a benefit.” The email went on to say that the benefit is a $1 discount code for the ParkMobile app.

First, the payment is only good for credit towards ParkMobile service fees (not even the actual parking fee), so you have to park at a ParkMobile-owned lot to use your benefit. Second, you have to enter the code you received manually in your account. Third, you can’t use your $1 all at once.

Your code is good for 25 cents off a ParkMobile service fee, the email explained, and it can be used up to four times, equaling $1. When I searched a few ParkMobile lots near me, service fees were between $1.80 and $4.

Industry observers note that naturally, users who received the email were quick to criticize. Several Reddit posts appeared, with users pointing out that you had to pay significantly more than your benefit to actually use it, claiming the settlement was just a ploy for lawyers to get paid, and some saying they thought the email was a phishing attempt.

Customers who received a $1 code have one year to use it.

#14322. The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
  • It has been revealed that the report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used.
  • The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

It has been revealed that the report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot highlighted that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a upcoming research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the firm (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

It has been revealed that METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

It has been revealed that though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” states Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”.

Kapoor claims he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor notes. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

It has been revealed that even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the newly introduced report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

In a recent development, but because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” claims Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”.

Recent findings suggest that matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he noted in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”.

Sources indicate that in general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

In a recent development, it’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how swiftly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor states. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.
  • All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent.
  • In a recent development, nominees are vetted in committees first, and then require majority approval from the Senate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Senate committee chaired by Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted today to approve a Federal Communications Commission nominee, despite accusations that the nominee gave false testimony about her work as a legal advisor for FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Democrats attempted to prevent a quorum by not showing up, but Cruz proceeded with a Republican-only vote.

All 15 Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted to approve Trump nominee Danielle Thumann, while the committee’s 13 Democrats were absent. “We’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs,” Cruz said at today’s hearing.

In a recent development, nominees are vetted in committees first, and then require majority approval from the Senate. Republicans are hoping to get Thumann confirmed before Democrats take Senate control in January.

Although the Senate Commerce Committee generally requires one minority member to be present for nomination votes, a spokesperson for Cruz remarked Senate rules allow the nomination to be advanced for a vote in the entire chamber. A spokesperson for Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the committee, said in response that “since 2005, Commerce Committee rules required that a quorum include one member of the minority for official action on bill, resolution, or nomination.”.

Sources indicate that technically, the committee has operated with no rules during Cruz’s chairmanship because Cruz “failed to pass committee rules” for the current session of Congress, Cantwell’s spokesperson said. “Nevertheless, in practice it has operated in line with rules from the last Congress (and this provision, specifically, since 2005), including that a quorum with a member of the minority party must be present for official action on a nomination or legislation. Until today.”.

At a hearing last week, Thumann mentioned she never worked with Carr on media-related topics, leading to accusations that she provided false testimony. “I have not worked with the chairman on any media-related concerns,” Thumann said after Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked, “Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?”.

Recent findings suggest that “It appears that Ms. Thumann misled the Committee and offered false testimony, seriously calling into question her judgment and character and impeding the Committee’s work in determining whether she should be seated on the Commission,” Luján wrote in a letter to Cruz yesterday. “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related concerns,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media-related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount.”.

According to recent reports, the FCC website describes Thumann as senior counsel to Carr on matters before the Wireline Bureau, the Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau, and the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau. Emails obtained in a public records request by the group Protect Democracy show she had some involvement in media-related matters.

Thumann provided follow-up responses to senators’ questions this week. She said that her work sometimes includes “reviewing documents or filings in a matter outside of my designated portfolio. However, I did not have any conversations with Paramount, CBS, or Skydance related to the merger.”.

Thumann has been referred to as Thumann Severs in the nomination process, but she uses the name Thumann.

Luján wrote that Thumann “played a role in processing informal complaints related to” alleged news distortion on CBS’s 60 Minutes, and that “she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” However, Thumann was only a recipient of the Kimmel-related emails we found in a search of the messages.

It has been revealed that the emails do show that Thumann approved language used in a response the FCC gave to complaints about the alleged news distortion in a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. The response informed people who submitted complaints that they should instead submit comments on an FCC docket that had been set up for the 60 Minutes proceeding.

Industry observers note that “Hi Kristi, I have confirmed with the Chairman and Erin that we would like for complainants to be encouraged to resubmit their news distortion complaints in the relevant ECFS [Electronic Comment Filing System] proceeding,” Thumann wrote. “Can you please work on some draft language to send to consumers that would advise them on this step (including how to use ECFS)?”.

Democrats revealed yesterday that they would try to prevent a quorum for today’s vote. They objected to adding a third Republican to the committee while a Democratic seat remains empty.

“All Democratic members of the Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee object to the majority stacking independent commissions with Republicans and rushing nominees through the Committee process in this lame duck session with no Democratic pairs,” Cantwell remarked in a statement.

Cantwell and other Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Cruz urging him to cancel the vote, while quoting his own words from 2014. “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the Democratic committee members said.

According to recent reports, cruz said today that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January. But today is November 18.” Cruz said there is “ample precedent” for advancing nominations in a lame-duck session.

Senate Commerce Committee rules state that a quorum for nomination votes requires a “majority of the members, which includes at least one minority member.” But a Cruz spokesperson pointed to certain clauses regarding committee quorums in Senate rules when contacted by Ars today.

Recent findings suggest that in the Standing Rules of the Senate, paragraph 7 of rule XXVI says that “no measure or matter or recommendation shall be reported from any committee unless a majority of the committee were physically present,” and does not have any requirement for minority members to be present. Elsewhere, the Senate rules say that when a committee reports a measure to the Senate floor, “no point of order shall lie with respect to that measure” as long as the committee took its action “in conformity with the requirements of paragraph 7 of rule XXVI.”.

While committees can have different quorum rules, a Cruz spokesperson said this functions as a “cleansing clause” so that “earlier procedural irregularities, such as a violation of a committee rule, cannot be used to invalidate the vote on the Senate floor.”.

FCC nominations have traditionally been paired with one Republican and one Democrat when there is an empty seat for each party. But Cruz mentioned that’s not a requirement.

“There’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs… the law merely states that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party,” Cruz stated during the Republican-only meeting.

According to recent reports, the Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority. It indicates, “The maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”.

Industry observers note that republicans would have a 3-1 majority on the FCC if Thumann is confirmed by the Senate. The sole Democrat, Anna Gomez, would have to leave at the end of 2027 if Trump does not nominate her for another term.

Recent findings suggest that “There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks… Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner,” Democrats told Cruz in their letter this week.

Industry News: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
  • It has been revealed that across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade.
  • Industry observers note that yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

It has been revealed that across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Industry observers note that yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

In a recent development, “I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”.

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, states cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory states he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”.

Industry observers note that given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most major outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” notes João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”.

According to recent reports, in the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a massive cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the manufacturer’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that in other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.

Sources indicate that it can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech tech giant may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.

Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with concerns. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.

When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.

When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.

According to recent reports, even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she claims.

Industry observers note that most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.

Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.

It has been revealed that even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the Internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.

In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.

If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It’s going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”.

Recent findings suggest that aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved swiftly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”.

In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.

Industry observers note that in the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?

For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don’t think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory states.

“If you’re immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don’t really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what’s different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.25047v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Options on VXX bring the dynamics of the VIX futures curve into the joint SPX-VIX calibration problem. We construct a common model by specifying the VIX and then recovering instantaneous SPX variance from the requirement that its risk-neutral conditional expected average over the next thirty days equals the squared VIX. With truncated signatures of time-extended polynomial diffusions, this recovery reduces to finite-dimensional linear algebra and gives explicit access to the futures underlying VXX. The same specification therefore governs equity variance and rolling volatility exposure. To accommodate flexible specifications while respecting variance nonnegativity, we develop a regularized model and quantify the pricing errors of its tractable VIX and VXX proxies. Applications to short-dated option smiles illustrate joint calibration across the three markets, with Monte Carlo estimates of the proxy error bounds well below quoted bid-ask spreads.

💡 Key Takeaways

In a recent development, amazon Route 53 now offers Private Endpoint Health Checks, enabling business-critical workloads that never touch the public internet, such as internal APIs, databases, and self-hosted nodes behind internal load balancers or in private subnets, to use native health monitoring and automatic DNS failover. Customers can health-check any reachable private target by IP address, domain, or port over HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP. Customers can associate these health checks with Route 53 DNS records across routing policies in private hosted zones, so Route 53 routes traffic only to healthy endpoints and manages failover automatically.

Previously, teams built custom control loops using Amazon CloudWatch alarms, AWS Lambda functions, and the Route 53 API to achieve DNS failover for private resources. With this approach, failover took several minutes and added operational burden. Detection and DNS failover with Private Endpoint Health Checks are designed to complete in seconds rather than minutes, the service is fully managed, and nothing is exposed to the public internet.

Sources indicate that the feature supports on-premises and hybrid endpoints reachable from the VPC over AWS Direct Connect or AWS Site-to-Site VPN, enabling resilience patterns such as active-passive disaster recovery and cross-Region DR over AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN. Amazon Route 53 Private Endpoint Health Checks is available today in all AWS commercial regions. To learn more, visit the Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide and the Route 53 pricing page.

Industry News: NASA's upcoming Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.
  • The moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon.
  • It has been revealed that these changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.

The moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit.

It has been revealed that these changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.

According to recent reports, for Starship, the evolved initiative has SpaceX fueling a Starship lunar lander in low-Earth orbit before docking with Orion in high-Earth orbit. The crew will fly to the Moon on board Orion before two of the four astronauts transfer into Starship for a landing on the Moon.

According to recent reports, due to the docking configuration with Starship, Orion must now fly backward to the Moon, with its Service Module at the top of the stack. This is a fundamentally different flying posture than Orion was designed for, Shireman noted, and creates problems for Orion’s propulsion system.

Sources indicate that as a result, the Service Module, which is provided by the European Space Agency, will require modifications to its propellant tanks. This is because liquid propellant would move toward the gas inlet side of the tanks, rather than settling in the direction expected during normal operation.

According to recent reports, “When you push it the other way, the liquid goes to the gas end of the tank, and you don’t want the liquid in the gas part,” Shireman stated. “Bad things can happen to you.” To address this, he said, the European Space Agency and its main contractor, Airbus, are modifying the vehicle’s tanks for Starship lunar missions.

NASA and Lockheed engineers have also been studying the impact of increased acceleration on Orion when the vehicle is attached to Starship. Under Orion’s original mission architecture, the spacecraft would experience accelerations of about 0.1 to 0.15 g during the translunar injection burn, Shireman said. But with Starship providing the thrust, the acceleration would increase to approximately 0.8 to 1 g, acting in the opposite direction from the one originally planned.

Orion’s structure must be certified to handle a substantially higher acceleration in the opposite direction, Shireman said.

Sources indicate that before astronauts land on the Moon, NASA is also planning a mission in low-Earth orbit to test Orion’s interactions with the lunar landers. Shireman mentioned this change in plans for Artemis III, declared earlier this year, has created new hazards, as Orion was not designed to spend more than a short period of time in low-Earth orbit.

Heating is a concern, he noted, because Orion was designed for deep space, which is colder than the thermal environment closer to Earth. For example, he said, Orion has passive thermal features designed to prevent the spacecraft from getting too cold in deep space. One of these is a silver-looking exterior tape that dissipates electrical charge and limits the radiation of heat into space. As a result, some of this tape will be removed for the Artemis III mission.

Engineers are also analyzing how to manage electrical loads to reduce heating and protect the avionics and crew cabin.

Industry observers note that another big change that stems from spending approximately two weeks in low-Earth orbit is the orbital debris environment, which is more congested than in deep space. Shireman mentioned NASA and Lockheed have not completed their assessment of the orbital-debris risk associated with the new mission profile. This should be done by January, and, if the risks are too high, it might lead to modifications of Orion’s orbit for the mission.

In a recent development, “There’s going to be a higher risk from an MMOD standpoint,” Shireman remarked of orbital debris near Earth. “It’ll be higher risk than flying out to the Moon.”.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, NASA removed the lunar landing from Artemis III, turning the mission into a demonstration of rendezvous and docking operations in low-Earth orbit. The agency is now targeting 2027 for the mission, leaving Orion and the lunar landing companies with a compressed schedule to complete substantial technical integration work.

It has been revealed that this may seem like a fairly straightforward process, but docking is rather complex. It involves mechanical capabilities like hooks, connectors, and pins; there are thruster-plume interactions with the landers, including possible damage from hot or abrasive exhaust; concerns about whether Orion’s laser system might incorrectly interpret reflections from surfaces on Starship or Blue Moon; and more.

Industry observers note that “We were going to do that work, but not on Artemis III, and not for both of the landers,” Shireman said of docking with Starship and Blue Moon. “It was going to be spaced out, so all that work gets crunched into this time frame.”.

Lockheed is working closely with NASA to prepare Orion to maintain an Artemis III schedule for a launch in summer or fall of 2027.

“We’re working three shifts,” Shireman said. “We had a zero-margin schedule already, so we’re, I call it hand-to-hand combat. Literally every day we’re clawing to see, ‘Hey, can we save a shift here? Can we save half a shift there?’”.

Shireman said he supports the urgency of Isaacman and NASA in their contest with China over the Moon. But it is important to keep an eye on mission safety, said Shireman, who worked at NASA during both the Challenger and Columbia accidents.

“We also have a responsibility to not go too fast and cut too many corners and make sure that we are not taking undue risks,” he said.

#14315. Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout.
  • The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day.
  • The ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watched other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn’t watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature.

The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them.

The ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents’ excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.

In a recent development, how did they get the mice to fight? “Mice are naturally territorial,” co-author Jorge Iravedra-Garcia of Princeton University told Ars. “A traditional behavioral assay that experimenters use is called resident intruder. You just drop mice that are bred to be slightly weaker, and a little bit more docile, into the home cage of strains we know are more on the aggressive side. Those strains are typically very good at just naturally evoking that behavior.”.

Industry observers note that so the fights weren’t entirely fair. “We tip the scales in favor of having a clear winner and a clear loser by having the clear winner be at home, be bigger, and be more experienced,” co-author Annegret Falkner, also of Princeton, told Ars. “We really wanted to show that these changes are adaptive in some way. Animals don’t know what the outcome of a fight is before they enter it. So we set up a situation where the outcome is a little bit more uncertain for the mouse.”.

In a recent development, the results: The spectator mice ended up being better prepared for fight night—despite being weaker, less aggressive strains—because they watched fighter mice during the training sessions. Specifically, both spectators and fighters spent less time with their backs turned toward opponents than novice mice, and were also quicker to attack. They also used similar moves. Granted, they weren’t quite as skilled as their fighter-mouse brethren; practical experience still mattered. But they learned enough through observation to perform better than the novices.

It has been revealed that that behavioral change was mirrored in the neural data: the brains of the spectator mice altered to more closely resemble the brains of the fighting mice across all 12 of the interconnected regions. During training, the spectator inhibitory cells resembled a fighter’s, while the excitatory cells were closer to those of novice mice, but that changed on fight night, when both types of cells more closely resembled those of fighting mice.

It has been revealed that “When you’re watching a fight, you’re paying attention to many things at once,” said Iravedra-Garcia. “You’re not just simulating that aggressive behavior in your head, you’re also trying to gauge who’s dangerous, who’s not, who’s actually involved in the fight versus ‘Do I know them? Are they novel to me?’ Witnessing aggression leaves a circuit trace that changes how an animal behaves in its next conflict, and that trace looks similar to the one left by fighting itself.”.

“They can watch males walking around all they want and none of this happens,” mentioned Falkner. “There’s something specifically salient and arousing about attack that makes them both want to attend to it and also drives this specific plasticity mechanism. That’s one of the open questions: why is attack so sticky? Probably because it creates these adaptive behavioral changes.”.

There have been similar studies, notably with macaques. According to Falkner, this latest study adds to that body of research by pointing to a specific mechanism for the learned behavior. “There’s this broad decrease in regions that are known to provide inhibitory control for some of these aggression control networks,” she said. “This one piece of the aggression network is really just the tip of the iceberg in terms of how global networks for aggression control respond during these observed activities. I think these subcortical subnetworks are really recurrent. It’s a tiny piece of a larger network.”.

Industry observers note that it’s an open question whether such findings in mice could extend to humans. “Although it’s difficult to draw a one-to-one parallel, these circuits are extremely conserved, especially these brain regions that seem to show this robust change in inhibitory tone,” remarked Falkner. “We think about violence as being maladaptive in human culture, but if you are a mouse or an animal who’s around a lot of aggression, it’s actually highly adaptive for you to be ready to fight at any particular time.” The same could be true of humans.

The authors blueprint to extend their research to determine whether female mice watching male mice duking it out changes their mating preferences. They also want to try to artificially induce the same brain activity changes and corresponding behavior. “It doesn’t seem that far-fetched to me,” remarked Falkner. “I think we know the state that the circuit needs to be in to execute this particular behavioral strategy. So whatever pattern of stimulation we can use to kick this plasticity mechanism into gear seems reasonable.”.

According to recent reports, nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9  (About DOIs).
