Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army unveiled late Thursday that it would delay a strategy to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air.
  • The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs).
  • It has been revealed that “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army unveiled late Thursday that it would delay a strategy to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Now the Army looks to wait until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

It has been revealed that “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”.

Telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”.

Lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army said. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”.

In an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army noted that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”.

Sources indicate that the military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it mentioned the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

Sources indicate that in all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” plan the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army stated the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”.

According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the proposal is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

Sources indicate that the Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

In a recent development, modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

According to recent reports, during the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed. It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

The Army’s plan was to communicate clearly with the public about the looks, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

In its environmental risk assessment, the Army stated it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”.

Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the strategy.

“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

On Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the plan “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.”.

Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:.

The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”.

Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.
  • Recent findings suggest that wireless industry lobby group CTIA stated a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Recent findings suggest that wireless industry lobby group CTIA stated a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:.

In a recent development, the pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA said the pilot test indicates “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”.

The FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr remarked. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”.

The Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC says its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

Carr said that “contraband cell phones continue to pour into prisons by the thousands each year,” with “estimates indicat[ing] that as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to these devices.” He said the phones have been used to plan scams, drug trafficking, and violent attacks.

“In Georgia, an incarcerated gang leader directed a drive-by shooting that killed two 13-year-old boys at a birthday party,” Carr said, referring to a 2024 shooting.

Carr defended the plan against criticism that it will block legitimate communications outside the prisons, saying it includes safeguards to prevent that.

According to recent reports, “Those that want to use the technology will apply to the FCC, explain how they proposal to deploy it, and show through testing that it stays inside the designated area and doesn’t interfere with lawful communications outside the prison walls,” Carr said. “Communities nearby will receive notice before operations start. We’re also seeking comment on next steps, including ways to close remaining loopholes on other frequencies and the possibility of quiet zones around correctional facilities.”.

Freedom of the Press Foundation Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern noted the FCC should have considered the benefits of contraband phones being used to document abuses inside prisons.

Industry observers note that “Prisons are the most secretive government institutions in the country and people wishing to expose abuses and inhumane conditions from the inside often do not have many options,” Stern wrote in a letter to FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez’s office, which was included on the FCC docket. “Last year’s Oscar-nominated film, The Alabama Solution, used footage incarcerated people captured with contraband cell phones to show Americans some of the awful things that go on in state prisons that they’d have no other way of seeing. The same footage bolstered an ongoing DOJ investigation into Alabama prisons and was crucial evidence in a civil lawsuit by Steven Davis, who was brutally killed by prison guards, that eventually settled.”.

Jamming contraband cellphones was supported by prison phone companies ViaPath (aka Global Tel*Link) and NCIC Correctional Services, the National District Attorneys Association, the Correctional Leaders Association, and National Association of Police Organizations.

“Inmates have used these phones to coordinate attacks against correctional officers and their families, as well as inmate violence, strikes, disturbances, and full-scale riots,” the National Association of Police Organizations noted. “They also use contraband phones to organize deliveries of illegal drugs and weapons into correctional facilities. These dangers underscore the need to authorize indoor jamming in state and local correctional facilities.”.

Gomez, the only Democrat on the three-member commission, remarked she’s concerned about potential unintended consequences, but voted with Republicans to allow jamming after safeguards were added to the order.

“For the last 90 years, the Federal Communications Commission has prohibited jamming by non-federal actors and even prohibited jamming equipment to be introduced into the American market,” Gomez said. “That is because jamming devices are specifically designed to interfere with communications devices in order to render them un-usable.”.

Gomez noted that “jamming can prevent devices from completing 911 and emergency calls as well as interfere with communications networks used by fire, police, Emergency Medical Services, and other public safety entities.” She also said making jamming equipment available in the American market could lead to “unauthorized sale of this hazardous equipment,” and that “the accessibility of jamming equipment can itself motivate criminal enterprise.” Criminals have used “Wi-Fi jammers to disrupt security systems, security cameras, and cellphones to conduct robberies at homes and at stores,” she said.

Gomez remarked she’s glad the final order includes safeguards “to ensure that jamming is contained to this unique use, to permit jamming by a very limited category of authorized actors, and to take as much care as possible to prevent jamming and jamming equipment from becoming a hazard to safety.”.

According to recent reports, gomez partially dissented because she is worried the FCC will let correctional facilities and prison phone companies charge higher prices for inmate calling services that connect inmates with family members. Under US law, the FCC sets limits on those prices and considers prisons’ and jails’ safety and security costs when deciding how much money they can charge, she said.

It has been revealed that gomez mentioned, “While correctional facilities should have safety and security services like jamming to prevent criminal activity, it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay for the costs of these measures… Jamming is specifically designed to block communications and is certainly not necessary to provide phone and video calls for incarcerated individuals. We should have made this clear in today’s order. Because we failed to do so, I dissent in part.”.

According to recent reports, the FCC order could be challenged in court. The CTIA has argued that the FCC “has no authority to allow jamming” under the Communications Act, which directs the FCC to prevent interference.

AT&T mentioned the FCC’s legal justification “is premised on a fundamental factual error: the assumption that jammers will only block ‘unauthorized’ communications without impacting lawful uses. There is no way to jam some communications on a spectrum band but not others. That is because radio jammers ‘block all wireless communications on affected spectrum bands,’ and, as the FCC has noted in the past, ‘cannot differentiate between contraband devices and legitimate devices.’”.

AT&T remarked that “there is simply no way to limit the reach of jammers to the confines of a given facility. Jammers have been shown to cause interference outside the facilities in which they operate, greatly increasing the risk that someone living or traveling nearby will be impacted.”.

AWS CloudFormation Service-Managed StackSets adds custom execution roles with nested stacks support

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (261 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS CloudFormation StackSets now supports custom execution roles for service-managed stack sets, which enables you to scope the permissions StackSets uses in each target AWS account.
  • Sources indicate that with a custom execution role, you define what StackSets can do in each account.
  • Recent findings suggest that to get started, choose Set execution role when you create a stack set in the CloudFormation console, or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs.

AWS CloudFormation StackSets now supports custom execution roles for service-managed stack sets, which enables you to scope the permissions StackSets uses in each target AWS account. StackSets deploys the same infrastructure, such as networking and security settings, across thousands of accounts and Regions in one operation. With a custom execution role, you can also use nested stacks, macros, and transforms in service-managed stack sets, which allows you to deploy the reusable templates you use for individual stacks across your organization.

Sources indicate that with a custom execution role, you define what StackSets can do in each account. By default, service-managed stack sets use a role in each account that can provision any resource in a template without additional setup, and that default remains available. Now, you can provide a template that defines an IAM role, called the execution role, and StackSets creates it in each account before deploying. For example, a stack set that creates Amazon S3 buckets can use an execution role limited to CloudFormation and Amazon S3 permissions. When you revision the execution role template, StackSets updates the role in every account it deployed to.

Recent findings suggest that to get started, choose Set execution role when you create a stack set in the CloudFormation console, or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. To learn more, visit the documentation and the AWS DevOps Blog. This feature is available at no additional charge in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. Refer to the AWS Region table for details.

Saddle up: Your dreams for 2030 just became possible for 2026.

According to recent reports, years ago, some leading researchers told us that their objective was AGI. Eager to hear a coherent definition, we naively asked âhow do you define AGI?â. They paused, looked at each other tentatively, and then offered up whatâs since become something of a mantra in the field of AI: âwell, we each kind of have our own definitions, but weâll know it when we see it.â.

It has been revealed that this vignette typifies our quest for a concrete definition of AGI. It has proven elusive.

While the definition is elusive, the reality is not. AGI is here, now.

Coding agents are the first example. There are more on the way.

Long-horizon agents are functionally AGI, and 2026 will be their year.

Before we go any further, itâs worth acknowledging that we do not have the moral authority to propose a technical definition of AGI.

Sources indicate that we are investors. We study markets, founders, and the collision thereof: businesses.

Given that, ours is a functional definition, not a technical definition. Upcoming technical capabilities beg the Don Valentine question: so what?

The answer resides in real world impact.

AGI is the ability to figure things out. Thatâs it.*.

*We appreciate that such an imprecise definition will not settle any philosophical debates. Pragmatically speaking, what do you want if youâre trying to get something done? An AI that can just figure stuff out. How it happens is of less concern than the fact that it happens.

A human who can figure things out has some baseline knowledge, the ability to reason over that knowledge, and the ability to iterate their way to the answer.

An AI that can figure things out has some baseline knowledge (pre-training), the ability to reason over that knowledge (inference-time compute), and the ability to iterate its way to the answer (long-horizon agents).

Sources indicate that the first ingredient (knowledge / pre-training) is what fueled the original ChatGPT moment in 2022. The second (reasoning / inference-time compute) came with the release of o1 in late 2024. The third (iteration / long-horizon agents) came in the last few weeks with Claude Code and other coding agents crossing a capability threshold.

Sources indicate that generally intelligent people can work autonomously for hours at a time, making and fixing their mistakes and figuring out what to do next without being told. Generally intelligent agents can do the same thing. This is new.

Sources indicate that A founder messages his agent: âI need a developer relations lead. Someone technical enough to earn respect from senior engineers, but who actually enjoys being on Twitter. We sell to platform teams. Go.â.

The agent starts with the obvious: LinkedIn searches for âDeveloper Advocateâ and âDevRelâ at competing companies â Datadog, Temporal, Langchain. It finds hundreds of profiles. But job titles donât reveal whoâs actually good at this.

It pivots to signal over credentials. It searches YouTube for conference talks. It finds 50+ speakers, then filters for those with talks that have strong engagement.

It cross-references those speakers with Twitter. Half have inactive accounts or just retweet their employerâs blog posts. Not what we want. But a dozen have real followings â they post real opinions, reply to people, and get engagement from developers. And their posts have real taste.

The agent narrows further. It checks whoâs been posting less frequently in the last three months. A drop in activity sometimes signals disengagement from their current role. Three names surface.

It researches those three. One just announced a upcoming role â too late. One is a founder of a company that just raised funding â not leaving. The third is a senior DevRel at a Series D company that just did layoffs in marketing. Her last talk was about exactly the platform engineering space the startup targets. She has 14k Twitter followers and posts memes that actual engineers engage with. She hasnât updated her LinkedIn in two months.

According to recent reports, the agent drafts an email acknowledging her recent talk, the overlap with the startupâs ICP, and a specific note about the creative freedom a smaller team offers. It suggests a casual conversation, not a pitch.

Total time: 31 minutes. The founder has a shortlist of one instead of a JD posted to a job board.

Industry observers note that this is what it means to figure things out. Navigating ambiguity to accomplish a goal â forming hypotheses, testing them, hitting dead ends, and pivoting until something clicks. The agent didnât follow a script. It ran the same loop a great recruiter runs in their head, except it did it tirelessly in 31 minutes, without being told how.

To be clear: agents still fail. They hallucinate, lose context, and sometimes charge confidently down exactly the wrong path. But the trajectory is unmistakable, and the failures are increasingly fixable.

In last yearâs essay, we wrote about reasoning models as the most notable new frontier for AI. Long-horizon agents push this paradigm further by allowing models to take actions and iterate over time.

Coaxing a model to think for longer is not trivial. A base reasoning model can think for seconds or minutes.

Two different technical approaches seem to both be working and scaling well: reinforcement learning and agent harnesses. The former approach teaches a model intrinsically to stay on track for longer by poking and prodding it to maintain focus during the training process. The latter designs specific scaffolding around the known limitations of models (memory hand-offs, compaction, and more).

Scaling reinforcement learning is the domain of the research labs. They have made exceptional progress on this front, from multi-agent systems to reliable tool use.

Designing great agent harnesses is the domain of the application layer. Some of the most beloved products on the market today are known for their exceptionally engineered agent harnesses: Manus, Claude Code, Factoryâs Droids, etc.

Sources indicate that if thereâs one exponential curve to bet on, itâs the performance of long-horizon agents. METR has been meticulously tracking AIâs ability to complete long-horizon tasks. The rate of progress is exponential, doubling every ~7 months. If we trace out the exponential, agents should be able to work reliably to complete tasks that take human experts a full day by 2028, a full year by 2034, and a full century by 2037.

Industry observers note that soon youâll be able to hire an agent. Thatâs one litmus test for AGI (h/t: Sarah Guo).

You can âhireâ GPT-5.2 or Claude or Grok or Gemini today. More examples are on the way:.

Medicine: OpenEvidenceâs Deep Consult functions as a specialist.

Law: Harveyâs agents function as an Associate.

Cybersecurity: XBOW functions as a pen-tester.

DevOps: Traversalâs agents function as an SRE.

GTM: Day AI functions as a BDR, SE, and Rev Ops leader.

Recruiting: Juicebox functions as a recruiter.

Math: Harmonicâs Aristotle functions as a mathematician.

Semiconductor Design: Ricursiveâs agents function as chip designers.

AI Researcher: GPT-5.2 and Claude function as AI researchers.

This has profound implications for founders.

Industry observers note that the AI applications of 2023 and 2024 were talkers. Some were very sophisticated conversationalists! But their impact was limited.

The AI applications of 2026 and 2027 will be doers. They will feel like colleagues. Usage will go from a few times a day to all-day, every day, with multiple instances running in parallel. Users wonât save a few hours here and there â theyâll go from working as an IC to managing a team of agents.

Sources indicate that remember all that talk of selling work? Now itâs possible.

What work can you accomplish? The capabilities of a long-horizon agent are drastically different than a single forward pass of a model. What fresh capabilities do long-horizon agents unlock in your domain? What tasks require persistence, where sustained attention is the bottleneck?

Recent findings suggest that how will you productize that work? How will your application interface evolve in your domain, as the UI of work grows from chatbot to agent delegation?

Sources indicate that can you do that work reliably? Are you obsessively improving your agent harness? Do you have a strong feedback loop?

How can you sell that work?Can you price and package to value and outcomes?

Itâs time to ride the long-horizon agent exponential.

In a recent development, today, your agents can probably work reliably for ~30 minutes. But theyâll be able to perform a dayâs worth of work very soon â and a centuryâs worth of work eventually.

What can you achieve when your aims are measured in centuries? A century is 200,000 clinical trials no oneâs cross-referenced. A century is every customer support ticket ever filed, finally mined for signal. A century is the entire U.S. tax code, refactored for coherence.

The ambitious version of your roadmap just became the realistic one.

Amazon EventBridge Scheduler expands its AWS SDK integrations with 589 new API actions across 81 AWS services, and adds templated targets for the enhanced EventBridge Custom event bus. You can now schedule direct invocations of a broader set of AWS services without writing custom integration code.

EventBridge Scheduler is a serverless scheduler that allows you to create, run, and manage billions of scheduled events and tasks across more than 270 AWS services, without provisioning or managing the underlying infrastructure. With a new templated target, you can schedule event delivery directly to the Custom event bus using its PutEvents or PutRawEvents API. The templated target also makes it easier to add metadata fields to each event. For example, you can send an event to your bus every night at midnight to start a reconciliation workflow, with no function in between to call the API.

The latest API actions are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon EventBridge Scheduler is available, subject to the availability of each target service in the Region. The templated targets for the Custom event bus are available in all AWS Regions where the enhanced Custom event bus is available. To learn more, see Using templated targets in EventBridge Scheduler and Using universal targets in EventBridge Scheduler in the Amazon EventBridge Scheduler User Guide. Install the Agent Toolkit for AWS to start building with your AI coding agent.

Today, AWS Billing and Cost Management announces upcoming APIs that let you view your AWS payment information through the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI. With these APIs, you can check your account balance, find invoices that are due or past due, see which payments and credit memos were applied to each invoice, and confirm that the payment methods on your account are active. You can call the APIs from your own tools or through an AI agent.

It has been revealed that previously, finance teams had to sign in to the console to find past-due invoices, match payments to invoices, or check whether a payment method was still active. Now you can automate these checks with APIs such as GetFinancialRecord, BatchGetFinancialRecord, ListFinancialRecords, GetAccountBalance, GetPaymentInstrument and ListPaymentInstruments. You can integrate the APIs with your accounts payable systems to monitor past-due balances and reconcile AWS invoices on your own schedule.

The APIs are available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and available to customers in all commercial AWS Regions.

To learn more, visit the AWS Payments API Reference.

#14260. Gig Work Is Invading Nursing Homes. The Risks Can Be Deadly

Gig Work Is Invading Nursing Homes. The Risks Can Be Deadly

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Within hours of being injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center.
  • In a recent development, felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived.
  • “It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Within hours of being injected with insulin that was meant for her roommate, 93-year-old Emma Lewis’ blood sugar plummeted, and she was rushed to a nearby medical center.

In a recent development, felicia Kaye, the licensed practical nurse who gave the injection in May 2022, was not an employee of Peachtree Centre, where Lewis lived. She was a gig worker who picked up her shift on the nursing app ShiftKey. She wasn’t familiar with Lewis or her roommate and never received orientation on any of the facility’s policies and procedures.

“It’s pretty much you get the keys [to the medication cart] and just figure it out yourself,” Kaye testified this August. Kaye declined to comment for this story.

It has been revealed that gig workers are flooding America’s understaffed nursing homes, resulting in a revolving door of staff caring for the nation’s elderly and infirm. ShiftKey boasts a network of more than 10,000 facilities—many of them nursing homes—and more than 200,000 health care workers hoping to fill shifts.

An investigation by Proof News and WIRED found that the gig nursing model is putting lives at risk: Numerous court filings, federal inspection reports, and interviews with former employees of the manufacturer, attorneys, and gig nurses themselves describe how ShiftKey thrusts workers into understaffed nursing homes with little to no onboarding—leading to dangerous situations.

In January, a federal surveyor from the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services noted that a ShiftKey worker made a mistake with a PICC line, a catheter threaded in a patient's arm to their heart. No one at the nursing home had checked that they were trained on the procedure. In 2025, a CMS surveyor wrote that a Texas nursing home didn’t orient temporary workers on how to feed residents before a ShiftKey worker tried to force feed one with a syringe. Later that year, a nursing home in Texas banned a ShiftKey worker after a resident who was supposed to be under her care was found sitting in urine and feces.

Inspection reports also reveal alleged abuse and theft. This summer at Hillsboro Rehab in Illinois, a ShiftKey worker allegedly stole the debit cards of two residents and used one of them at a local smoke shop and ice cream store.

In a recent development, according to the inspection report, the nursing home notified ShiftKey about the incident and blocked the worker in the app so they couldn’t pick up shifts there in the future. The worker was later arrested, and residents repaid, according to Tim Blythe, regional vice president of operations for Tutera, Hillsboro Rehab’s parent company.

“We sincerely regret this unfortunate incident,” Blythe wrote in an email. “We completed an internal investigation and notified the individual's employer, law enforcement, the Office of Inspector General, and appropriate regulatory agencies.”.

Sources indicate that one ShiftKey worker was accused of slapping a resident in the face in Texas in 2022, and another of “verbal abuse” of a resident in Tennessee in 2023. At the Center at Grande in Texas, a third was accused of stealing hundreds of dollars from four residents in February 2025. None of the facilities responded to a request for comment.

ShiftKey pitches itself as the Uber for nursing. “We applied technology to the nurse staffing industry,” reads an internal “selling points” memo obtained by Proof and WIRED. “What Uber did was connect the customer directly with drivers. ShiftKey connects facilities directly with providers.”.

“Our technology is part of the solution to [the] patient care crisis by allowing highly experienced nurses to work on the schedules they choose and by enabling healthcare facilities to quickly fill care gaps and deliver patient care,” ShiftKey CEO Mike Vitek noted in a statement to Proof News and WIRED.

Though ShiftKey advertises open shifts for a variety of facilities—including those for addiction treatment, psychiatric hospitals, and correctional institutions —a Proof News and WIRED analysis of 108,706 available shifts collected in March, July, and August 2026 found that 89 percent of open shifts were at nursing homes.

The app offers shifts for mostly lower-paid nursing staff. A majority of the open shifts Proof Upcoming and WIRED reviewed called for licensed practical nurses or certified nursing assistants, careers that don’t require a bachelor’s degree and are paid between $20 and $30 an hour on average, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

In his statement, Vitek disputed that the model is “harmful to the industry” given “long-standing, systemic concerns within the healthcare ecosystem.” He emphasized that ShiftKey verifies credentials, conducts background checks, checks abuse registries, and makes that information available to facilities.

“Importantly, training or orientation required by any facility to operate within its policies is conducted by that individual facility,” Vitek said. “At ShiftKey, we do not employ nurses—we simply enable their access to flexible shifts.”.

According to recent reports, like a growing number of platforms built to automate workforce management, ShiftKey relies on a variety of automation tools. The software allows facilities the option to automatically post and accept shifts; the app uses a “formula-based calculation” to assign workers a “reliability score,” according to Vitek, which nurses remarked affects their ability to get shifts; and it offers shift scoring, last-minute pricing, and dynamic pricing based on demand and supply, according to the tech giant’s job postings and employees’ professional profiles.

Sources indicate that but when a concern is raised, Vitek noted, a human reviews it. He said they evaluate claims of “medical malpractice or abuse, neglect, or exploitation of a patient as soon as ShiftKey receives it” and decide if deactivating the worker is “appropriate.” He declined to comment on these specific events, citing reasons of privacy and ongoing litigation. He added there may be instances where ShiftKey is not promptly notified, which can delay action.

After the insulin incident, Kaye testified, she wasn’t prevented from working on the platform.

Industry observers note that in court filings, both ShiftKey and Peachtree maintain they shouldn’t be held responsible for Lewis’ death. ShiftKey argued that it is not liable because Kaye “has never been its employee,” while Peachtree mentioned it “cannot be held liable for the acts of an independent contractor.” Kaye is not named as a defendant, and ShiftKey is paying $40,000 to settle with Lewis’ family.

A representative for Peachtree Centre declined to comment citing pending litigation. In court, the home pointed out Lewis was admitted to the hospital with many conditions besides effects from the injection, and her death certificate lists “senile degeneration of the brain” as the cause.

Industry observers note that as part of the case, Kaye testified that she drove more than 250 miles from Myrtle Beach to work the Peachtree overnight shift. She had over two years of experience at the time and said she wasn’t given so much as a tour before being the only nurse posted to oversee a floor of 22 patients.

“This particular shift I had a lot of patients,” she testified in the August deposition. “It was very overwhelming.”.

In their complaint against Peachtree and ShiftKey, Lewis’ family noted they’d entrusted their “vulnerable” mother to a home they expected to “properly train staff.”.

It has been revealed that “I’ll never get Mom back,” said Lewis’ son, James Lewis, in a deposition earlier this year. “I just don't want it to happen to anybody else.”.

According to recent reports, kara Smith can’t tell you where she’ll be working next week. A certified nursing assistant, Smith logs into the ShiftKey app most mornings to browse eight-hour shifts at more than a dozen long-term care facilities within driving distance from her West Virginia home.

According to recent reports, lured by the promise of scheduling freedom and premium pay for hard-to-fill shifts, Smith became a ShiftKey contractor in 2022. She claims she soon learned it's not unheard of to work night shifts at nursing homes staffed entirely by ShiftKey.

Founded in 2016 in Texas, ShiftKey grew rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, as unprepared nursing homes reeled from rolling outbreaks that could claim dozens of lives in a single facility. Health care workers sought higher pay as their risks mounted, and homes scrambled to fill shifts.

Sources indicate that backed by private equity, ShiftKey and its competitors Clipboard Health and IntelyCare benefited. According to an analysis by the US Department of Health and Human Services, from 2019 to 2022, the use of contract staff in nursing homes tripled from 4 to 12 percent of all nursing hours. Though it’s since declined, the rate remains higher than prepandemic.

In 2023, ShiftKey’s then CEO told Axios that the company was valued at more than $2 billion.

Industry observers note that nursing homes pay ShiftKey set rates for workers. The platform then “mathematically” calculates a “suggested” rate for each shift posted, Vitek mentioned in a statement, emphasizing that dynamic pricing tools are only used to increase pay for “difficult-to-fill” shifts—and never to decrease rates.

Workers then bid to claim it. This bidding system is what got Smith hooked: Instead of accepting whatever wage a facility would offer, Smith haggled for higher pay.

According to recent reports, “If I can even make 25 extra cents, I'm going to try to push for that,” mentioned Smith, a 47-year-old single mom. “Every penny counts.”.

Since the pandemic, however, wages on ShiftKey have plummeted, according to several nurses who spoke with Proof News and WIRED. Teresa, an LPN who declined to give her last name, joined ShiftKey in 2019. She stopped using the platform last year when she noticed competition for shifts growing—and pay rates declining.

“People were fighting over trash shifts for under $20 an hour,” remarked Teresa, a single mother of three kids.

Smith remembers being able to bid $3 to $4 more an hour above the facility’s suggested rate when she first joined, but this year she said she’s been forced to accept less money or risk no work at all.

According to her ShiftKey payment records that she shared with Proof News and Wired, one facility paid her $32.50 an hour in the summer of 2025 and around $26 a year later. Payments from another nursing home revealed the same downward trend. On Facebook groups, many ShiftKey workers have posted about a similar dip in earnings.

In a recent development, “The starting bids are shamefully low,” remarked Smith. “It’s not worth the workload or the drive.”.

Industry observers note that during her four years with ShiftKey, Smith said she routinely felt “thrown in” at upcoming facilities without orientation, clear instructions, or logins. She said she had to work hard to familiarize herself with the residents’ conditions, because critical details, such as who is a fall risk or who has a catheter or an ostomy, are frequently missing. Hours in, she felt like she was in “an ocean and nobody’s around me.”.

“We're coming there because they're short-handed,” noted Smith. “So we are automatically going to be walking into a shit show.”.

Smith said a lack of orientation led to scary close calls. Last year, she indicates she arrived at a Virginia nursing home with no advance information, not even the door code. She didn’t know anything about the patients, and that made her “very stressed out.”.

“I know my blood pressure went up because of it,” she said.

Another time, Smith said she dropped off a regular drink to a resident only to later learn that they were prescribed only thickened liquids to avoid choking.

“What if they choked and died?” stated Smith.

In a recent development, facilities on ShiftKey have the option to require that workers attend a paid “orientation shift” before picking up a regular one. But four ShiftKey workers told Proof News and WIRED that they've frequently picked up nursing home shifts without doing an orientation shift first.

Inspection reports from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services dating back to 2023 and obtained by Proof News and WIRED reveal ShiftKey workers making dangerous mistakes.

In Ohio, after a ShiftKey nurse made a PICC line mistake at Stellar Care Center, a federal inspection report noted that the nursing home’s administrators had never checked to see whether she was trained to do IV therapy.

The report noted that an administrator had spoken with someone at ShiftKey, who told her that because they consider everyone on the app an independent contractor, the firm didn’t test for what skills they knew.

Industry observers note that in other cases, the orientation was inadequate. At Woodway Rehabilitation and Healthcare Center in Texas, a federal health surveyor spotted a ShiftKey worker trying to force-feed a resident a health shake using an oral syringe. The ShiftKey worker said it was her first time at the facility, according to the 2025 inspection report. She received some orientation for the facility on the app before she started her shift, the report said, but couldn’t remember if feeding was included.

Recent findings suggest that in 2024, another CMS surveyor wrote that a ShiftKey nurse at the Medical Suites at Oak Creek in Wisconsin told the surveyor she was not shown any care aims for residents on her first day. According to the report, the surveyor spoke with an administrator, who handed the surveyor an undated orientation checklist. The administrator stated they did not right now have a policy regarding orientation for gig nurses, but that she'd be implementing one in 30 minutes.

Neither Stellar Care, Woodway Rehab, nor the Medical Suites at Oak Creek responded to requests for comment on this story.

Researchers warn that gig nurses who aren’t properly oriented and who move constantly between facilities can disrupt the continuity of care. Jasmine Travers Altizer, an assistant professor at Latest York University’s Rory Meyers College of Nursing, conducted a qualitative study of 22 nursing home administrators this year and found that they felt relying on temporary workers led to “less consistent care, more hospital transfers, potentially unnecessary treatments and antibiotic use, and increased falls.” Administrators also reported staff having less ability to support one another across the facility.

Gig nursing “shouldn't be a fix for chronic understaffing,” remarked Travers Altizer in an email. It's critical, she said, to “have consistent staff who know the residents.”.

In response, Vitek, the ShiftKey CEO, remarked, “Continuity of care is an important consideration in nursing home quality, but the matter predates platforms like ours.”.

It has been revealed that shiftKey states its model keeps more nurses on the job during a time of critical shortage. Vitek stated a survey of workers on ShiftKey found that more than a third stated they would not be able to stay in the health care industry without such a platform.

“We reject the premise that enabling independent flexible nursing support is harmful to the industry, because the challenge in addressing these issues is not about the choice between full-time staff versus temporary shift support,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that katie Wells, a researcher who tracks gig nursing, said a combination of factors made platforms like ShiftKey an attractive option for nursing homes. Health care facilities were struggling financially, and many of them had been taken over by private equity, which Wells said “contributed to lean staffing models that make facilities more likely to want to just plug the hole rather than invest in a larger staff.”.

According to CMS data, the average time worked by nursing staff per resident at Peachtree, where Lewis was accidentally injected, is lower than the state average and less than minimum requirements set by the US Department of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration that are no longer in effect. The American Health Care Association, a nonprofit group that represents nursing homes, successfully challenged the rule in court in 2025, and the Trump administration ultimately withdrew the rule, stating that the move would save nursing homes $55.1 billion over the course of 10 years.

Sources indicate that “We need to have minimum safe staffing levels,” said Hannah Garden-Monheit, who worked on nursing home reform at the White House National Economic Council and now is executive director of Columbia Law School’s Center for Law and the Economy. “The patients need that continuity of care.”.

Half a dozen ShiftKey nurses and the two former corporate employees told Proof News and WIRED that many of the facilities that use ShiftKey have a history of poor quality of care and staffing issues.

One ShiftKey nurse recalled rats scurrying in the ceiling and roaches falling from lights at one nursing home.

Constance Hicks, a longtime certified nursing assistant in Connecticut, noted that most nursing homes she worked at through ShiftKey were in terrible condition: no barrier cream, no soap, no supplies. Some places had no hot water. Not once in more than a year of picking up shifts through ShiftKey does she remember receiving any training at the homes.

Sources indicate that in November 2023, while working a double shift at Cobalt Lodge Healthcare, Hicks discovered an elderly patient with their head and neck trapped in a bed rail, their forehead compressed against the metal, according to court records. She checked the patient’s vitals and, finding dangerously high blood pressure, called 911. Even though her shift had ended, Hicks stayed until emergency workers arrived.

Hicks noted she documented everything and sent it to ShiftKey. She also tried reaching out to the organization’s representatives but said no one responded. By the next day, her ShiftKey account was deactivated.

Hicks, who says the incident with the patient caused “a whole lot of psychological trauma,” tried to file a lawsuit against ShiftKey over the deactivation and other issues, but court records show the company successfully moved her case to private arbitration.

Cobalt Lodge Healthcare did not respond to a request for comment, and ShiftKey declined, citing ongoing litigation.

Regarding the quality of the facilities, Vitek said, “When professionals raise a concern, we encourage them to use the formal reporting channels, and remind them that they can choose whether they can accept future shifts there.”.

Some lawmakers have begun scrutinizing platforms like ShiftKey, in part over concerns that it’s misclassifying its workers as independent contractors.

A gig nurse logs into ShiftKey.

“It's not like they're coming in, bringing their own tools, fixing a pipe, and leaving,” says Emma Greenman, a Minnesota state representative, of gig nurses. “They are being managed by somebody.”.

ShiftKey disputes that characterization. “ShiftKey, as a technology marketplace, does not employ healthcare professionals but connects them with healthcare facilities that have gaps in their schedule,” said Vitek, adding that the tech giant works “tirelessly” to ensure its model complies with the law.

Greenman is working on a bill that she mentioned would curb worker misclassification in Minnesota, including in gig nursing.

“What they’re doing is building business models to evade, break, and distort labor law for profit,” Greenman noted.

There’s also the glitch of whether to allow nursing homes to staff largely with gig workers. The year Lewis died, an analysis of staffing data submitted to CMS shows that nearly a third of the total nursing staff hours at Peachtree were performed by temporary workers.

Gary Poliakoff, one of the attorneys representing Lewis’ family, said that some weeks, the rate of temp workers including ShiftKey rose to as high as 50 percent of all nursing staff.

With little orientation, Poliakoff said, the model puts both patients—and workers—at a “great disadvantage.”.

After the mistaken insulin injection, James Lewis said he got the call from Peachtree letting him know his mother was in the hospital. According to his deposition, he was getting ready to go to church to preach and planned to visit her later. He often went every day. They’d eat lunch together and watch The Price Is Right, but that day he was looking forward to spending some time outside. It was Mother’s Day.

When asked if he knew that Peachtree sometimes had temporary workers, he responded that he wasn’t aware.

In a recent development, “I don't know if it was a traveling nurse or what,” he noted in the deposition. “But I know it wasn't a regular person.”.

It has been revealed that in her testimony, Kaye blamed understaffing for her insulin mix-up. She remembered working at Peachtree twice in November 2021 but went six months without returning because she thought it was a “shithole.”.

“It was not a nice facility by any means,” Kaye said.

She testified she was already an hour late giving the insulin, having too much on her plate.

It has been revealed that “I remember being not helped at all by administration, not knowing who anyone was,” said Kaye. “And pretty much being by myself.”.

Ben is a founder of Prod, which has quickly become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley. Asher, one year Benâs senior, is a former debate champion turned Stanford statistics Ph.D. The brothers have an eye for raw talent, and aged 25 and 26 respectively, they are building the âyoung personâs AGI lab.â Their co-founder Aidan Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at Neuralink for three years while in college at Georgia Tech. Ben and Asher believe that raw talent â the type of people who would previously have gone on to do Ph.D.s or join quant firms â are the key to unlocking the next phase of AI development. This stands in sharp contrast to the approach of focusing on âbrand nameâ AI talent at any price, which seems so in vogue right now.

There is something else that is countercultural about this lab too: they recognize that scale alone is not enough. Indeed, the lab is predicated on this notion. There is only one Internet, and weâve run out of it. Data is the bottleneck today to further AI scaling, not compute. Todayâs AI models are wildly inefficient, something that Dwarkesh Patel has recently hammered home in his interviews with Andrej Karpathy, Richard Sutton and others. Flapping Airplanes is dedicated to searching for a more data-efficient AI. The companyâs name is a nod to a more biological notion of machine intelligence.

One of the fundamental debates right now in AI is around scaling vs. research. The scaling paradigm argues for dedicating a huge amount of societyâs resources, as much as the economy can muster, toward scaling up todayâs LLMs, in the hopes that this will lead to AGI. The research paradigm argues that we are 2-3 research breakthroughs away from an âAGIâ intelligence, and as a result, we should dedicate resources to long-running research, especially projects that may take 5-10 years to come to fruition.

While the divide between these two schools of thought is far from absolute â research breakthroughs make compute investments more efficient, and GPUs are required for net fresh research â they each lead to different tradeoffs. A compute-first approach would prioritize cluster scale above all else, and would heavily favor short-term wins (on the order of 1-2 years) over long-term bets (on the order of 5-10 years). A research-first approach would spread bets temporally, and should be willing to make lots of bets that have a low absolute probability of working, but that collectively expand the search space for what is possible.

One concern I have had is that by starving Ph.D. programs of talent, and by reallocating a lot of this talent to scale-oriented work (as opposed to fundamental research), we could actually push out the AGI timeline. As I noted in a previous blog post, âcorporate politics tends to favor in vogue, consensus ideas over more radical, unpopular ones â the very kinds of ideas that can take years to prove worthwhile, and which scientific breakthroughs often depend on.â Flapping Airplanes is explicitly intended to provide a Ph.D.-like experience â true research independence, long-time horizons â while bridging the pay gap between academia and Big Tech.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest learnings of the last decade in AI is the dramatic economic value of fundamental scientific progress. Since academia seems ill-suited to compete with Big Tech on this dimension right now, especially in AI, Flapping Airplanes is taking this into their own hands. And they are focused on precisely the problem that is likely to define the next wave of AI: building models inspired by the data efficiency of biology. With that as a north star, the firm will make bets in a variety of directions to get there.

There are two coherent motives right now in AI. One is the profit motive, and this should inspire all application builders, given the tremendous opportunity ahead. As I have noted on many occasions, AI is so underpenetrated relative to the capability set available, it is likely to create a golden age for builders for many years to come. There is a large profit pool available, and we are in the very earliest stages of generating it.

The second coherent motive in AI is AGI, predicated on the belief that now that weâve unlocked a machine intelligence, we should push toward upleveling that intelligence. Economically, progress in this direction is likely to be extremely valuable. The question is how to take on this objective in an efficient way, with a reasonable probability that resources invested will translate into long-term positive results. Flapping Airplanes is a pure play in that direction.

One of the most attractive aspects for me in partnering with Flapping Airplanes was the team. I have met nearly every candidate that has interviewed at Flapping Airplanes, and certainly every person the company has hired. This is one of the best teams Iâve ever seen assembled at the beginning of such an ambitious journey.

There are two core beliefs that make Flapping Airplanes different for top talent:.

A belief that young people have always unlocked fundamental science in the past (Einstein was 26 during his âMiracle Yearâ).

A conviction that AI research is not a mystical domain for experts, but a domain learnable by anyone that is smart and ambitious.

With just these two premises, Flapping Airplanes is at odds with a prestige-obsessed culture in the Valley right now. It is exactly this obsession with substance and with raw individual talent that made Ben so successful at Prod, and it is this âflame spottingâ ability that gives me confidence in the courageous effort that is now Flapping Airplanes.

#14256. ‘The Hairiest 90 Minutes of My Career’: How the FAA Ground Stop Went Down

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1193 w)

‘The Hairiest 90 Minutes of My Career’: How the FAA Ground Stop Went Down

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Wednesday of this week—six days after a 4.5-hour nationwide ground stop that panicked onlookers and scrambled air travel—US transportation secretary Sean Duffy remarked he still wasn’t quite sure what led to the Friday meltdown.
  • Recent findings suggest that still, the Federal Aviation Administration has revealed that a few things did go wrong on Friday afternoon.
  • The agency has since described the ground stop as something executed “out of an abundance of caution.” On Wednesday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford appeared to downplay the incident even as he took blame for it, calling the outage “a knee scrape, and I’m sorry.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Wednesday of this week—six days after a 4.5-hour nationwide ground stop that panicked onlookers and scrambled air travel—US transportation secretary Sean Duffy remarked he still wasn’t quite sure what led to the Friday meltdown. “The root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet,” he said after a meeting with lawmakers.

Recent findings suggest that still, the Federal Aviation Administration has revealed that a few things did go wrong on Friday afternoon. It involved routine infrastructure replacement, a faulty router, data overload, and disruption in some regions in the radio communications that air traffic controllers use to speak to each other and pilots.

The agency has since described the ground stop as something executed “out of an abundance of caution.” On Wednesday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford appeared to downplay the incident even as he took blame for it, calling the outage “a knee scrape, and I’m sorry.”.

While aviation industry workers maintain that flyers were safe throughout the ground stop, some felt government officials downplayed the event, which left air traffic controllers scrambling to backup frequencies even as they tried to figure out what was going on.

“That was the hairiest 90 minutes of my career,” one air traffic controller told WIRED.

Contacted for comment, FAA spokesperson Steve Kulm didn't answer questions but referred WIRED to the agency’s ground stop Q&A web page, where the agency writes it has “clear, established, standard procedures to ensure safety during incidents such as this.” It says that some radio frequencies and radar feeds remained online during the communication problems, “allowing air traffic controllers to maintain communication with and track aircraft.”.

Here’s what we know about the ground stop so far.

To understand the communications concerns that led to the ground stop, here’s a quick overview on how air traffic control works.

It has been revealed that most flyers are familiar with the towers near airports, officially called the Airport Traffic Control Towers (ATCT). The controllers who work here manage aircraft ground movements, including takeoffs and landings. Once an aircraft gets up into the sky, around 10,000 feet, it’s passed to controllers in a Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) center, who manage airport arrivals and departures. Then, once a flight is really underway, an aircraft is passed to Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often just called Centers. There are 22 of these in the US, and controllers there guide airplanes for most of their flight, passing off the aircraft as they move between regions.

Recent findings suggest that the communication radios used at Centers have a range of around 150 miles—a problem when the areas they have to manage are more than 100,000 square miles each. So phone lines at the Centers lead to networks of transmitters, each installed remotely.

For decades, this network has been connected by copper telecommunications lines—outdated and sometimes brittle tech. So in 2025’s GOP-led Big Beautiful Bill, the Transportation Department received the billions of dollars in funding needed to upgrade that copper to fiber-optic cables. The upgrade swaps the system, the private communications backbone of Air Traffic Control, from one of mechanical switches to a digital system built on internet-based protocols. A contractor called L3Harris—the network owner—manages the transition, and as of last week, the project was about 70 percent complete. This was where the FAA ran into problems.

In a recent development, the trouble began in El Dorado, Arkansas, the site of one of those remote communications facilities, which is part of the larger Center based in Memphis, Tennessee. There, the FAA says a contractor with L3Harris was making on Friday what is now a routine switch from that legacy copper system to a fiber-optic one. But something, it appears, went wrong when the worker plugged in a newly introduced router as part of that transition, and the FAA still doesn’t know why.

Data began to flood the network, making 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to the FAA. The agency states another remote site, a radar-based facility in Amarillo, Texas, may have also flooded the network with data. To compensate, the network tried to recruit other nodes, and they got overloaded, too, taking down several radio frequencies on the network.

Recent findings suggest that at first, the concern manifested as intermittent dropouts on radio frequencies at Centers in the region, from Kansas City to Chicago, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to WIRED under the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the press. This made it difficult, if not impossible, for air traffic controllers to talk between Centers and with pilots through normal channels. From there, though, the problems seem to have cascaded to other regions, including the areas around Washington, DC, and New York.

Sources indicate that in control rooms—mostly Centers dealing with en route flights—air traffic controllers first noticed some “dropouts” on their radio transmissions, according to two sources. On their own, these sorts of communication disruptions aren’t unheard of. But when they began to spread to multiple regions, FAA officials really began to pay attention.

Because officials didn’t understand why the radio frequencies were unstable, the agency called a nationwide ground stop.

One person who spoke with WIRED noted they still had access to a backup frequency during the network instability. The FAA said “some frequencies and radar feeds remained reliable.”.

According to recent reports, then, according to the FAA, contractors from L3 Harris blocked data from the remote Arkansas and Texas locations from the wider network. That restabilized the system, restoring radio contact between everyone in the airspace.

In a statement Friday, a spokesperson for the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, a union that represents almost 20,000 controllers, wrote that “air traffic controllers were on the job, carrying out their responsibilities and working to ensure the safety of the National Airspace System.”.

While the technical concerns led to several uncomfortable hours for aviation professionals, midair passengers remained safe during the ground stop, says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San Jose State University in California. “It was certainly an abnormal situation, but it wasn’t an emergency, because we’ve trained for it,” he says. “It was not dangerous, but it was highly inconveniencing, and it was not normal.”.

It has been revealed that it helped that the radio outage did not seem to have affected all Centers, and even fewer TRACONs and local towers. That means pilots were generally in contact with controllers, especially as they circled airports and landed their planes.

It also helped that pilots don’t actually need air traffic control to fly their planes, Miller says. “Talking to a controller is not what keeps an airplane in the sky,” he says. Pilots have plenty of systems onboard that allow them to “see” what’s going on around them.

In a recent development, despite the lack of clarity on what exactly happened with the newly installed router to make it malfunction, Duffy has settled on a solution: more money. On Wednesday, he officially asked Congress for $50 billion, with $30 billion of that dedicated to air traffic control modernization.

So whether you’re shopping for a fitness lover or someone who could use a little self-care, there’s likely a Therabody gadget worth wrapping up.

I haven't yet tried every product in the Therabody lineup (I’m getting there), but I've put most to the test and am ready to recommend my favorites. Plus, most are FSA/HSA-eligible and designed with USB-C charging capability.
