Sources indicate that updated November 2026: I’ve added the Theragun Prime (6th Gen) and removed discontinued products. I also confirmed up-to-date links and prices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

If you’re looking for a professional-grade massage device, the Theragun Pro Plus is one of the most advanced percussive guns on the market, incorporating vibrations, heat, and near-infrared LED therapies for an all-in-one recovery tool. It also offers cold therapy, but you'll have to purchase an additional attachment for $100 to make use of that capability—a steep add-on for what is already a splurge. After testing the attachment myself, I don't think it justifies the cost unless you are sure you'd regularly use the contrast therapy.

In a recent development, priced at $650, this is the most expensive Theragun, so I'd recommend it to athletes or those who are dealing with chronic muscle pain and want the LED therapy. For casual consumers, some of the features might feel like overkill. For example, there's a built-in biometric sensor for heart rate tracking that I have barely used. I do, though, appreciate the OLED screen, which displays a force meter, so you can see exactly how much pressure you're applying. It's a useful function if you need a nudge to apply more pressure or a reminder to ease up.

The Theragun Prime (6th Gen) hits the sweet spot between the elite Pro Plus and the budget-friendly Relief. It’s still a premium percussive massage gun, with five speed settings, two attachments (a dampener and standard ball), and up to 120 minutes of battery life. You won’t get extras like heated or near-infrared LED therapy, or compatibility with Therabody’s cold and vibration attachments, but you will enjoy top-notch durability. It’s the only Theragun in the lineup rated to withstand drops from up to 10 feet, making it an excellent gift for the accident-prone person in your life.

Industry observers note that the Theragun Relief, introduced in 2023, remains the cheapest Theragun—priced even lower than the Mini Plus. For the price tag, you’re sacrificing some of the premium features, like the LCD screen and Bluetooth connectivity to the Therabody app for device control. But you can still follow guided routines on the app, and the simple one-button control is refreshingly simple to use.

Industry observers note that the Relief comes with three head attachments and has three speed settings, which is a step down from models that offer a standard five speeds and four or more attachments. Still, the Relief is less than half the weight of the Pro Plus, and it's equipped with the essentials, which is more than enough for the average person.

The original Theragun Mini is still a solid portable device—and it's $60 less—but the Mini Plus feels like a shrunken version of the elite Pro Plus. The ergonomic triangular design lets me target trigger points and muscle groups like my hamstrings and calves with more pressure control (though, admittedly, that same shape makes it awkward to use on my lower back). Thoughtful details, like a travel lock to prevent it from powering on and a compact carrying pouch, make it easy to carry on commutes and flights.

Most notably, it brings heated percussive therapy to a travel-friendly device. The heat therapy is easily my favorite feature on the Pro Plus. The Mini Plus is also compatible with Therabody's Vibration Plus and Cold Plus attachments (both sold separately).

Recent findings suggest that note: Some customers have reported charging complications, saying their units wouldn't power up, but I haven't run into any battery problems in my two weeks of testing. I'll revision this review if anything shifts with long-term use.

The JetBoots Pro Plus are full-length, wireless boots that combine pneumatic compression with vibration therapy and infrared LED light. Everything is controlled from a built-in LCD screen and control panel on the lead boot, and connectivity is effortless, automatically linking when powered on.

According to recent reports, eight preset programs target legs, knees, and joints, but you can manually adjust pressure, intensity, and the session length. Sessions can run from 10 to 60 minutes in five-minute increments, with compression adjustable between 20 and 100 millimeters of mercury (mmHg)—a standard unit of measurement for pressure. Vibration offers three intensity levels (low, medium, and high), and the infrared LED setting is a simple on or off, with an automatic shutoff after 45 minutes.

In a recent development, inside the boots, a nonporous proprietary material reduces moisture and microbial buildup, and after months of testing, I haven't noticed any lingering odors. These are best suited for athletes, frequent travelers, or anyone managing circulation-related conditions. Conveniently for those aforementioned jet-setters, the JetBoots Pro Plus are TSA-approved for carry-on travel; just keep in mind that they're pretty hefty.

I enjoyed the original TheraFace Mask, but the upgraded TheraFace Mask Glo feels like the smarter purchase. It's easier to find (Therabody seems to be phasing out the original), costs $270 less, and is slightly lighter at 1.13 pounds versus the OG's 1.27 pounds. While the Glo has fewer LED bulbs—504 compared to 648—the difference doesn't translate to a lesser treatment. You get the same red, infrared, and blue light wavelengths, plus the signature vibration therapy that made the first-generation mask stand out.

The vibrations are now integrated into the adjustable straps rather than the mask itself. They're usually distracting, occasionally even headache-inducing, depending on my mood. I usually skip the vibration setting altogether to make this component less irritating. Even without it, the Glo remains competitively priced among high-end LED masks.

Treatment sessions range from four to 12 minutes, and the removable eye shields are thoughtful, but I prefer taking them off to extend the light coverage to my under-eye area. I very much appreciate the cordless design, but I do miss the display stand that came with the original. I often end up storing it back in its box, which makes me less inclined to reach for it. If you, too, deal with this concern, you might consider buying a travel case for $80.

I challenge you to stay awake through a full session with the SmartGoggles 2.0. I’ve been testing them for months, and more often than not, I conk out while wearing them. The combination of gentle heat, vibration, and massage therapy across my forehead, eyebrows, and temples relaxes my facial tension within minutes. I love wearing them when I have a headache from staring at screens all day, and while I don’t struggle with regular migraines, I can see them being a soothing blackout remedy in a quiet, dark room.

According to recent reports, former reviewer Medea Giordano loved the first model, and this upgrade improves the fit with contoured padding that feels similar to Therabody’s SleepMask. You still get three preset modes: Focus, Sleep, and SmartRelax. That last option uses biometric feedback to adjust vibration patterns based on your heart rate. It also syncs with the Therabody app, letting you tweak the vibration and heat intensities or incorporate sound therapy. Note, though, if you’re a side-sleeper, you’ll have to shift around, as these are most comfortable while lying flat on your back.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve tested several sleep masks, and the TheraFace SleepMask is among my favorites. Many claim to be 100 percent blackout, but this one leaves me feeling totally disoriented when I wake up, with no idea what dimension I'm in—just how I like it. The contoured padding feels plush, and the adjustable strap keeps the mask in place without tugging at my hair, even when I shift around at night. It comes with a carrying case, so I always pack it for travel.

Industry observers note that the selling point is that this mask uses vibrations—three pattern presets (Pulse, Wave, Constant)—designed to nudge your brain into deeper rest. I struggle with staying asleep, but when I wake up in the middle of the night, I just tap the button to start a 15-minute session, and it usually lulls me back to sleep. That remarked, the vibrations are almost too gentle; you barely feel them, but you can absolutely hear them. It's not as soothing as a white noise machine, so if you're a light sleeper, this might be a deal-breaker.

Industry observers note that the TheraFace Depuffing Wand has become a staple in my travel bag. It delivers both hot and cold therapy to help reduce puffiness, improve circulation, and enhance product absorption before completing your skin care routine. It’s TSA-friendly—zero awkward bag checks and counting—and ideal for tackling under-eye bags after a long flight or night. The curved applicator reaches every contour of my face, and the precision tip is great for trickier spots like under my eyes. It’s intended to be used on clean, dry skin, so I hold the opposite side of my face to prevent tugging.

It has been revealed that the wand comes with three preset temperature levels that feel gentle but effective. While the cold function isn’t as icy as a roller fresh from the freezer, it’s consistent throughout a six-minute session and doesn’t drip. Plus, this one won’t crack if you forget to take it out of the freezer (RIP to two of my traditional rollers). An indicator light flashes at three minutes to remind you to switch sides, but this notification is easy to miss if you’re not looking straight into a mirror.

Industry observers note that cupping is an ancient healing technique that uses suction to provide muscle relief. Therabody's version combines suction, heat, and vibration therapy for localized recovery. With three levels of suction (30, 40, and 50 kilopascals, or kPa), three heat intensities (41, 43, and 45 degrees Celsius), and three vibration modes (low, high, and wave), I appreciate how you can customize the intensity of your session. The TheraCup is also programmed with an auto-shutoff after three minutes—so you don’t overdo any area—and built-in safety sensors that will cut off the pressure if it exceeds 60 kPa.

TheraFace Mask for $650: The TheraFace Mask is a cordless, hands-free light-therapy device that uses three wavelengths (red, infrared, and blue) to tackle different skin care goals. As a distinguishing feature from its competitors, the TheraFace Mask includes a built-in vibration therapy mode that massages pressure points around the eyes, brow line, and scalp for some added stress relief. It comes with removable eye shields and a sleek display stand, which makes it easy to store on your nightstand.

JetBoots Prime for $550: Compared to the JetBoots Pro Plus, the JetBoots Prime is simple to use: You get four pressure levels (25, 50, 75, and 100 mmHg) and three durations (20, 40, or 60 minutes), all adjustable throughout your session through a built-in control panel. Th boots are wireless with a 180-minute battery life and can even be used while charging. Plus, they fold down into the included drawstring bag, making them portable and fuss-free to stow away.

Industry observers note that waveRoller for $180: Foam rollers are great for improving range of motion, increasing blood flow, and reducing muscle tension. You can buy a decent foam roller for significantly less, but with the WaveRoller, you get Therabody app integration for a personalized experience and five vibration frequencies. Designed for full-body use, it works best for warm-ups and post-workout recovery.

Theragun Mini (3rd Generation) for $220: I recommend the Mini if you’re new to percussive therapy or need something packable for travel. It's the smallest and lightest Theragun, with three attachments (standard ball, dampener, and thumb) and a soft-zip case that fits into a tote, gym bag, or carry-on.

It has been revealed that theragun Sense for $300: The Theragun Sense is slightly smaller (and lighter) than the Pro Plus, and it’s also impressively quiet. Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

Why the best founders are âtime travelersâ who play all three phases simultaneously.

In the Prod community, they talk about founders as âtime travelersâ rather than visionaries. Founders donât see the future, they teleport there.

According to recent reports, I think this is true in more ways than first meets the eye. To extend the analogy of a chess game (which I recently used in an essay on the AI race and which Will Manidis also articulated beautifully in his essay on âEndgame Playâ), outside observers see startups as temporally sequential, with a beginning (inception/ seed stage), middle (product-market fit/ growth stage), and end (IPO/ scale-up). However, the best founders actually live in all three of these phases simultaneously.

Opening: The opening phase of a startup involves the âmagicâ of transforming from a few people with an idea into a âstartup.â Silicon Valley excels at this magic, and Paul Graham is the prophet of the opening. There are many opening strategies, but the lean startup model has proven itself to be the most repeatable one. The ecosystem around tech giant formation is vital because foundational decisions made at this stage are difficult to change later, and so wisdom pays dividends.

Midgame: The midgame of a startup begins once product-market fit has been reached. Many startups fail before ever reaching this stage. Product-market fit requires deeply understanding a customerâs need, and building a solution. Once product-market fit has been reached, you need to build a company â figure out how to hire people, manage people, and improve the product. You need to achieve some type of takeoff, forward momentum that will allow the business to grow from something tiny and irrelevant into something meaningful and important. Board members exist to transmit inter-generational knowledge on midgame play. Since the nature of the midgame is always evolving, founders need to filter this through their own prism to arrive at truth.

Industry observers note that endgame: The endgame of a startup is the infinite future â itâs never really reached. The endgame is key, because without a vision of the future, the present has very little value â see the recent SaaSpocalypse. Elon Musk is the prophet of the endgame, he has always focused on the hardest problems, knowing that ambitious problems attract excellent people and unleash them to do their best work.

Some startups seem uniquely engineered for the opening, some for the midgame, and some for the endgame. A hot AI manufacturer from Stanford students is engineered for the opening game â they will easily be able to recruit friends and a bike ride to Sand Hill road easily yields capital. A vertical SaaS company is engineered for the midgame â getting off the ground is hard and recruiting the early team is challenging, but once you unlock PMF, thereâs a clear path for how to scale it up. And a deep tech company is engineered for the endgame, itâs always clear from the moment of inception why that company should pass the âwho cares?â test.

Every startup has a different set of challenges depending on what parts of the game are structurally easier and harder. For example, a startup with a weak endgame story will struggle to raise funding without immense traction. A startup with a strong opening story is at risk of hubris, employees thinking the firm has reached the promised land, when nothing substantial has been achieved. And the âvalley of deathâ is famous in deep tech, precisely because a strong endgame story is always preceded by a long, fatigued midgame. The #1 piece of advice I give friends who are starting companies is to be aware of these biases, and explicitly combat them.

What is so incredible about the best companies, and the best founders, is that they appear to be playing the opening, midgame and endgame simultaneously. In the best companies, it is always early days and there is a significant dream ahead (the opening vibe), even many years in. This is how Clay feels, even though the tech giant is almost ten years old. Similarly, the best startups often have midgame characteristics at the opening â within a few months, they can show traction and improvement, creating a sense of forward momentum. For example, RunwayMLâs incredible open-source growth, years before Stable Diffusion. And finally, the best companies create a feeling of inevitability early, such that employees genuinely feel like they are moving the world forward. For example, Anduril pioneering modern defense tech.

Recent findings suggest that one phrase Iâve often used to describe the best founders is, âNo matter what happens, they are going to win.â Alex Wangâs incredible journey at Scale from strength to strength was an early and illustrative example of this concept for me. The journey of Crusoe from crypto miner to AI factory builder is another great story of grit and judgement. What has crystalized for me now is seeing a superstructure that makes this possible â these founders are constantly holding the opening, midgame and endgame in their minds at the same time, and hence they are able to create a flexible, nimble culture that is always reinventing itself, and they are much quicker in adjusting their business strategy when the times are changing.

Sources indicate that my advice to founders is therefore this: No matter where you are in your journey, donât think about your business sequentially. Force yourself to play all three games at once â when planning product decisions, when making hires, when pitching investors. If you are in the midgame, you still need to care about opening style hires that could change the business. If you are in the opening, you need to think about the endgame, because thatâs what will inspire others to join you and help turn your vision into reality. And if you are in the endgame, you should still care about midgame momentum and opening creativity â thatâs how you will become absolutely massive. As you build your company, each of these narratives should be getting stronger â you canât just focus on the one that seems immediately in front of you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One afternoon in the fall of 2023—fifteen days after Hamas’ brutal October 7 attacks—the founder of the right-wing news aggregator Visegrad24, Stefan Tompson, texted a confidant to work out some private thoughts on what he called “the Israel situation.” Over the previous two weeks of carnage in the Middle East, Tompson’s team had pulled off a social media coup, and now he seemed to be wrestling with how to wield his channel’s newfound influence.

Almost from the moment Hamas paragliders first touched down in Israel, Visegrad24—then a three-year old Polish account ostensibly dedicated to “curating news, politics, current affairs, history, and culture from Central and Eastern Europe”—had managed to swoop in and dominate X’s breaking-news discussion of the war in Gaza.

In the conflict’s first three days, V24’s team worked around the clock to pump out nearly 400 posts on the violence: a mix of terse news updates, soft tributes to Israeli victims, and—above all—rage-bait videos showing allegedly “pro-Hamas” demonstrations in cities across the West. According to a rapid analysis that month by media researchers at the University of Washington, those 400 posts racked up an astonishing 370 million views. As the UW researchers framed it, a 641,000-follower Polish account had just catapulted itself atop a list of “latest elites” on X, momentarily trouncing the reach of legacy outlets with follower counts in the tens of millions, like CNN, The New York Times, and the BBC.

It has been revealed that more to the point, Visegrad had also established itself overnight as one of the most influential pro-Israel accounts on X. And that’s what seemed to be giving Tompson pause.

Recent findings suggest that “With the Israel situation,” Tompson texted his colleague, “I do loathe Hamas, and it’s been the perfect excuse to show the scale of Muslim infiltration in the west” (a long-standing editorial priority for Tompson and his team). But Tompson seemed wary that Israel was already angling for a wider regional conflict. “Personally I want that war to be contained where it is,” Tompson wrote. “And the Israelis do seem to be doing some vicious things.”.

Ultimately, the founder reasoned a way through his qualms. In another message from the same day, the cigar-smoking, cravat-wearing, thirtysomething Tompson wrote to the same confidant—whom I’ll call Boris—to spell out how he’d landed with regard to V24’s “editorial line” on Israel. As Tompson saw it, V24 had been faced with “four options” once the war started:.

Sources indicate that 1. Say nothing;2. Be objective—get hated by both sides;3. Pro Muslim—there are 1.5 billion of them;4. Pro Israel—There are fewer but also they have a lot of influence and money.

In choosing between those options, Tompson laid out a blunt motivation: “My goal is to fundraise off of this,” he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that covering Gaza did fit nicely with V24’s long-standing brand of anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, Western-chauvinist content. (“The beauty of this war is that it allows us to criticize slims—especially those in Europe—without any consequences,” Tompson would later write, using a shorthand slur for Muslims.) But now he seemed to have his eyes on a bigger opportunity: using Visegrad’s “upcoming elite” status to rake in money from some of Israel’s most powerful supporters in Silicon Valley and beyond.

And according to an extensive trove of V24 financial records, internal communications, screenshots from group chats, and correspondence with donors, all reviewed by WIRED, Tompson promptly succeeded at exactly that.

Over the past six years, Visegrad24 has become a strangely ubiquitous force in right-wing social media, its feed a reliable kaleidoscope of dehumanized, brown-skinned aggressors and their alleged depredations against innocent, often white-skinned victims, alongside global news from a nationalist perspective. On any given day, V24 might show you a stomach-turning video of a camel being abused at a wedding in the West Bank, a parade of cell phone clips showing violent crimes being committed by alleged “migrants” all across Europe, or an interview about the Great Replacement Theory.

From its headquarters in Warsaw, V24’s lean pseudo-news operation has proven itself almost preternaturally adept at virality on Elon Musk’s X. It even seems to have become one of the oligarch’s own favorite accounts. For a period after November 2024, Musk became especially fixated on British far-right politics, posting nonstop about “rape gangs” of South Asian men allegedly grooming British girls. To better understand Musk’s influences at the time, WIRED partnered with the research firm Bright Data to analyze his interactions with some 30 prominent European far-right accounts over a 45-day period ending in January 2025; we found that Musk engaged with Visegrad24, a major font of “grooming gangs” content, at least three times more than any other account on the list. Another dubious mark of distinction for V24: Of all the billion-plus accounts on X, Visegrad ranks 32nd in the number of community notes—crowdsourced fact checks—that have been attached to its posts.

Recent findings suggest that but in tandem with its drumbeat of demonized migrants, V24 has also excelled at capitalizing on the information wars that inevitably form around real, bloody conflicts like those in Ukraine, Gaza, and now Iran. The documents obtained by WIRED—to which Tompson responded with a blanket denial and an email from a lawyer—shed an intimate light on how this playbook evolved over the course of V24’s rapid rise. They provide an unvarnished case study of life inside today’s fractured and erratic right-wing mediasphere. And they reveal how the right kind of online influence, even when it’s strategically acquired by an entity just barely above the gutter of white nationalism, can command support from some of the most powerful people in the world.

In late November 2023, Tompson wrote to Boris with some exciting news. “Jewish VCs have created a group,” he texted. “Several. I’m in two of those groups that actively push back against founders who have supported Palestine.” In another message he described one of these encrypted text threads as “85 people. 84 Jews and me.”.

Recent findings suggest that “They are slowly reaching out directly … Usually they want a retweet,” he wrote to Boris. “V24 is such a significant part of the Israeli PR they all know what it is now.”.

“You’re in the belly of the beast now,” replied Boris (who requested anonymity for fear of legal retaliation).

One of the groups to which Tompson gained entry was called Jewish Alliances, described by one of its members—someone going by the handle Sean Rad, which is the name of a Tinder cofounder—as a space to “bring together Jews and non-Jews working together to fight antisemitism.”.

Sources indicate that on Jewish Alliances, Tompson came personally recommended by Shaun Maguire, a general partner at Sequoia Capital who led the firm’s investments in Elon Musk–affiliated companies. Like V24, Maguire had become vociferously pro-Israel after October 7—later explaining that the attacks galvanized him to engage in “information warfare” for the country. Maguire had even made introductions that eventually helped connect the Israel Defense Forces with Musk’s Starlink satellite communication network in the earliest days of the Gaza war. And now, on Jewish Alliances, he was throwing some weight behind V24.

It has been revealed that “Stefan / Visegrad is an incredible account if you’re not already following,” Maguire told the group thread. Privately, Maguire told Tompson, “I’ll give u $25k and try to raise the rest.” (Maguire later told WIRED that he ultimately had to stop short of making his donation. “I would have loved to donate to Visegrad, as I think their content is excellent, but I wasn't able to for compliance reasons.”).

Recent findings suggest that as for the other elite group chat that Tompson says he was invited to join, it appears to have been even more rarefied. In December that year, Tompson sent Boris a screenshot of a blurb from a Puck newsletter, headlined “The In-Crowd’s Hottest Text Thread.” Tompson had circled the item in red with an arrow pointing at it.

“I learned this week that hundreds of the most powerful figures from Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and Hollywood have joined a sprawling, informal WhatsApp thread to share thoughts on how to build support for Israel and combat antisemitism following the attacks of October 7,” wrote media reporter Dylan Byers in the blurb. “The group, which is called Builders for Israel, includes the likes of Sheryl Sandberg, Bill Ackman, and David Marcus.”.

“And Stefan Tompson 😂,” Boris replied, to which Tompson responded with his own laughing emoji.

Industry observers note that on the two group chats, Tompson sometimes gawked at the proceedings, sending Boris screenshots of what he was witnessing. On November 24, one member posted the following message to the group: “I bought some domains. If anyone would like them to redirect to appropriate content lmk.”.

The member then listed out a series of five urls: “longlivetheintifada.com, wechargeyouwithgenocide.com, palestineisourhome.com, fromtherivertothesee.com, fromtheriver2theseapalestinewillbefree.com.”.

“Btw this is available albeit $75k,” the member went on, before posting a screenshot showing a listing for the domain name “Allahuakbar.com.”.

Tompson himself responded inside the group. “Oh this has so much potential! 💀” he wrote.

(A review of public web domain records indicates that all five of the first urls listed here were registered through GoDaddy using Domains by Proxy, a service that allows domain registrants to hide their personal contact information. The records show that all five were created on November 22, 2023, in two batches 33 minutes apart. It’s unclear whether anyone bought Allahuakbar.com, whose owner is also hidden behind the proxy service, but its registration record was last updated on November 28, 2023.).

It has been revealed that as a platform for fundraising, the two group chats appear to have paid off pretty handsomely for Visegrad24. “Should have 75k on Monday,” Tompson wrote to Boris on November 18. There was $50,000 coming from “a very private man” at the Silicon Valley fintech investment firm Ribbit Capital. Ribbit's founder is Meyer “Micky” Malka, an early investor in Coinbase and promoter of crypto. Tompson would later tell Boris that Malka was allegedly planning to donate an additional $200,000. Financial records show donations of $50,000 and $200,000 roughly lining up with Tompson's messages, but Malka did not respond to requests for comment. Records indicate that Tompson also secured a $20,000 donation from the investment firm Hindenberg Research, with an additional $15,000 linked to an email address associated with the firm’s founder, the prominent Wall Street short seller Nathan Anderson. Tompson also claimed he had a “soft commitment” from the Israeli American investor Daniel Gross, a former AI lead at both Apple and Y Combinator. (Anderson did not respond to requests for comment; Gross’s representatives stated they have no record of a donation.).

Notifications from GiveButter, a site Tompson used for soliciting contributions, show that other donations were linked to email addresses associated with SimpleVenue CEO Michael Sinensky, Warby Parker founder Neil Blumenthal, Wix president Nir Zohar, Lux Capital cofounder Josh Wolfe, and deep tech venture capitalist Matt Ocko.

Industry observers note that (Sinensky and Blumenthal declined to comment, and Zohar’s representatives stated they had no record of him donating. Wolfe and Ocko neither confirmed nor denied that they’d given money to V24, but both came back with remarkably similar responses, primarily taking problem with WIRED’s characterization of whether Visegrad is “far right.” “I don't fund or support ‘far right’ groups,” Wolfe wrote, “and thankfully Stefan and Visegard24 are pro-democracy, pro-Western values, pro-peace and prosperity.” Wrote Ocko: “Even cursory research indicates that neither Mr. Tompson, nor Visegrad24 are affiliated with or support anything other than: classical liberal Western values, including the rule of law; the defense of democratic polities from terror and autocracies … peace and prosperity for all law-abiding and civilized people; opposition to horrific antisemitism and terrorist exaltation.”).

While Tompson was fundraising away with his group-chat contacts, Boris wrote with a question. “By the way, should I take Middle Eastern money?” he asked, mentioning opportunities to raise funds from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

“100 percent yes. Play both sides,” Tompson said. “I do the Jewish side. You do Arabs.”.

Recent findings suggest that to receive its donations, V24 set up an organization under the 501(c)(3) umbrella called the Intermarium Foundation, headquartered in Pennsylvania but domiciled in Delaware. Over the next year and more, over a million dollars poured in. Much of the money, including some of the largest sums, appears to have come in through “donor advised funds”—“dark money” philanthropic vehicles that allow donors to hide their identities, even from the recipients of their cash. Foundation documents show that in November 2024, the organization received $175,000 from DonorsTrust, a fund closely aligned with the Trump administration’s priorities, often referred to as the “dark money ATM” of the American right. Documents also suggest that V24 received $172,000 from the Giving Back Fund, which describes itself as a “national nonprofit organization that encourages and facilitates charitable giving by professional athletes, celebrities, high-net-worth individuals, existing nonprofit organizations, corporations, and others.”.

A London-born self-described “Polish South African” who was “educated in French schools,” Tompson founded Visegrad24 in early 2020. He'd moved to Warsaw from London in the mid-2010s, having worked as a PR strategist on the “Leave” side of the Brexit campaign, according to Gizmodo. Tompson’s great-grandfather, he has remarked, was the Polish ambassador to England at the time of the Nazi invasion. Between the war and the communist takeover of Poland, the family was left stranded abroad for three generations. In a 2024 interview with Jewish Insider, Tompson referred to his arrival in Warsaw as his “own version of aliyah,” the Hebrew word used to describe a Jewish person’s immigration to Israel.

According to recent reports, tompson’s homecoming took place just as Poland was attempting to aggressively pattern itself after Viktor Orban’s Hungary. In 2015, the illiberal, nationalist Law and Justice Party swept Polish elections and set about packing courts, hollowing institutions, and seizing control of Polish state radio, newspapers, and television—turning the latter into nakedly xenophobic, anti-opposition, and often antisemitic propaganda organs.

It has been revealed that with his taste for cravats and posh Barbour jackets, Tompson found an audience on Polish state TV documentaries extolling the country’s grand cultural heritage. He started a PR agency called Bracia Tompson SC, and according to the investigative site VSquare, he made short films with the support of something called the Institute for the Legacy of Polish National Thought, described by the Polish news outlet Polytka as a slush fund for the governing party.

Tompson also spent the late 2010s working on what he described as a “three-hour documentary” about his father’s ancestral home, South Africa—a country whose quality of life, Tompson claimed in a 2019 Polish radio interview, is worse today than under apartheid. The documentary project was reportedly titled African Volhynia, after an area in Central Europe where Poles suffered historic massacres, land dispossession, and ethnic cleansing—a framing that, to some observers, strongly suggests that Tompson was packaging a South African “white genocide” narrative for a Polish audience. The full documentary, however, was never released.

Instead, Tompson shifted focus to launch Visegrad24 in January 2020, with a logo closely mirroring the South African outlet News24. The name Visegrad is a reference to the Visegrad Group, an informal diplomatic bloc of four Central European nations that includes Poland and Hungary. In 2020, it was Poland’s turn to occupy the rotating presidency of the alliance—and V24 appears to have served a promotional function. When V24’s Facebook page was briefly blocked for violating community standards in 2021, the Polish deputy minister of foreign affairs spoke up for the account. “The Visegrad24 profile is not an official profile of the Visegrad Group or the Polish presidency of the Visegrad Group,” he told a Polish radio station. “However, we appreciate it for its promotion of the group’s activities.”.

One of Tompson’s main partners in the enterprise was a Polish journalist named Adam Starzynski, the former proprietor of an ultra-right-wing Twitter account called @BasedPoland and reportedly a fellow board member at something called the State of Poland Foundation. Their third, more silent founder was Tompson’s brother Jan. Tompson’s sister Alexandra also became involved, sometimes serving as a de facto legal rep.

In its early years, Visegrad24 posted roughly in line with the Law and Justice Party’s priorities—positively about Poland’s abortion ban, negatively about migrants, fulsomely about Christianity and Hungarian fertility rates—and was tagged frequently by party officials, according to Polish investigative site OKO.Press.

Industry observers note that but Tompson harbored bigger ambitions, as well as some apparent personal struggles. In early 2022, Visegrad’s core team escaped the Polish winter by renting a house together in the Canary Islands—during which time Tompson was said to be “undergoing acute drug withdrawal and was in a very vulnerable state,” according to an email later written by Alexandra and reviewed by WIRED. (In a couple of messages, Tompson refers to a time in his life when he was “on coke.”).

The team had been in Gran Canaria for about a month when something momentous happened: Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine. In the early morning hours of February 24, they woke up to images of Russian tanks crossing Ukraine’s borders. They immediately began pushing out an intense volume of news and clickbait.

Bit by bit, Visegrad started gaining international traction—and international notoriety for spreading fake news. On February 25, Visegrad tweeted “PornHub cockblocks Russian consumers,” alleging that Russian porn seekers “were presented with a message saying the content is blocked along with a Ukrainian flag and a message of support to Ukraine”—a rumor that was debunked by Snopes and other online fact-checkers. Then, about a week later, V24 tweeted that actor Leonardo DiCaprio had donated $10 million to Ukraine in honor of his grandmother from Odesa. (DiCaprio made no such donation, and there is no evidence of such a grandmother.) Articles debunking V24’s claim promptly appeared on Snopes and CNN.

This first brush with global virality came with risks. Elon Musk didn’t own Twitter yet, and content moderation was strict. “I’m really stressing out over v24,” Tompson wrote in an internal WhatsApp group named Gran Canaria. But rather than get shut down, V24 lived to see its follower count triple, growing from 80,000 to 250,000 in weeks.

V24’s boosted reach didn’t bring an end to Tompson’s frustrations, however. He appeared dissatisfied with the liberal followers that came along with being such a prominent pro-Ukrainian account. And he also seemed to be running into patronage problems: In 2022, the Polish news outlet Wiadomości revealed that the office of Polish prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki had tried to allocate about $300,000 for “the implementation of the public project titled ‘Visegrad24,’” sending money to a sports and fitness NGO called the Action-Life Foundation. Then, in 2023, according to OKO.press, Morawiecki’s office appears to have sent a bit under $600,000 for a “media center” at the Action-Life Foundation—which appeared, yet again, to be a carve-out for a V24-affiliated project. This time the grant was recalled after public outcry. (In an interview, Tompson has mentioned he “never had a penny to run Visegrad” from the Polish state.) In October 2023, the Law & Justice Party lost its majority in parliament, ending eight years of right-wing dominance over Polish government purse strings.

It has been revealed that by that fall, Tompson seems to have realized that V24’s Canary Islands posting blitz had yielded a huge bump in influence that they’d failed to monetize. In terms of fundraising, Tompson told Boris, “we missed the boat with Ukraine.” So when V24 repeated its flood-the-zone strategy with the October 7 attacks, Tompson seemed determined not to skip the next step.

By early 2024, Tompson was sitting down in Tel Aviv for a podcast interview with the American-born Israeli venture capitalist Michael Eisenberg—often billed as an informal adviser to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Less than six months had passed since October 7, and Tompson was on his way to becoming a minor celebrity among friends of Israel. “Meet the Man Who Shapes Millions of Twitter Users’ view of Israel’s war,” ran the headline of a story in the Jewish Chronicle, which went on to describe a series of V24 videos Tompson’s team had been filming on the streets of the West Bank. “Anyone who says it is an apartheid state in Israel and the Palestinian people are subjugated should go to Ramallah,” Tompson told the news outlet. “There were Maseratis and Mercedes and a brand-upcoming shopping mall.” As of that month, at least 28,473 Palestinians had been killed in Gaza since October 7, and at least 388 had been killed in the West Bank, Israel, and East Jerusalem, according to the United Nations.

According to recent reports, tompson was also busily fundraising. “The west is under attack,” claimed a sleek V24 donor pitch deck dated August 2024 and later reviewed by WIRED. “We face two major adversaries: radical progressives” and “nefarious States (Russia, Iran, China, Qatar).” The pitch deck called V24 “the frontier of modern journalism for western values.”.

One pitch deck promoted “Project Q,” a social media campaign against Qatar. In a single month, Project Q had delivered “97 posts about Qatar across multiple accounts,” 12 original pieces of video content, including a “viral” short featuring the British anti-Islamic activist Tommy Robinson, video essays, and an instance of then Polish MEP Michał Dworczyk condemning Qatar in a speech.

V24 also boasted that it was building “a network of Muslim and Arab influencers to push content,” including pro-Israel voices Loay Alshareef, Nuseir Yassin, Luai Ahmed, and YouTuber “Apostate Prophet,” the latter an ex-Muslim interviewee on V24’s YouTube.

In a recent development, then there was the Project Veritas–style hidden-camera news operation Tompson had launched, called V24 Investigations, run by the ex-Project Veritas board member Matthew Tyrmand. In the spring of 2024, V24 Investigations fanned out across American university campuses amid pro-Palestine protests to make unflattering, Project Veritas–style videos of student activists, part of a larger V24 effort to expand its YouTube presence.

But in 2025 and 2026, Visegrad would see more opportunity to draw on a traditional area of strength—breaking war news on X.

On June 13, 2025, Israel leaped into the wider conflict that Tompson had initially been afraid of: That morning, Tel Aviv brutally ambushed Iran with an onslaught of synchronized assassinations, air raids, and drone strikes—and V24 aggressively posted through it on X. But this time, alongside its fairly typical mix of war porn and mockery of pro-Palestinian protesters, a somewhat unusual motif ran through Visegrad’s social coverage of the war: Enthusiasm for restoring the leadership of Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last Shah.

Industry observers note that V24 even played a bit part in the social media war to influence US president Donald Trump as he toyed with joining Israel’s fight. On the fifth day of the war—after Trump had stated on Truth Social, “We know exactly where the so-called ‘Supreme Leader’ is hiding”—Visegrad chimed in with a post on X seemingly tailor-made to sweeten the option of regime change:.

Recent findings suggest that incoming reports of Iranian military officers seeking contact with Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi to declare their intent to defect. They also want to pledge their allegiance to His Majesty and his mission to lead the transition to democracy in Iran after the regime’s fall.

Visegrad’s post received more than a million views and was shared nearly 3,000 times.

When Trump finally did make his move four days later, dropping a set of “bunker buster” bombs on Iranian nuclear sites, V24 posted an image of the Islamic Republic’s flag being torn away to reveal that of the Pahlavi monarchy and the words “It’s time” (2.4 million views, 3,600 shares).

According to recent reports, why the outsize focus on the sexagenarian exiled son of a former dictator? Pahlavi does enjoy a certain amount of organic political support among the Iranian diaspora. But he’s also been held up at times as Israel’s preferred leader for Iran. In October 2025, Haaretz, TheMarker, and the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab reported that Israel’s government was likely behind a massive Persian-language “influence operation” to simulate online support for Pahlavi using bots, synchronized posting campaigns, and artificial intelligence—all “as part of an even broader Israeli campaign to influence the social media discourse.”.

Sources indicate that V24’s own pro-Pahlavi posting binge was underway at the same time. When asked whether V24 had received any funding from Pahlavi’s network, Tompson responded by saying, “I wasn’t aware that Reza Pahlavi was a foreign state.” When asked whether he had received any money from Israel directly, Tompson replied with an apparent joke. “Yes,” he wrote, “Benjamin Netanyahu personally hands me money for every post on Visegrad24.”.

In the three years since October 7, Visegrad24’s follower count has swelled to 2.1 million on X. But even as Musk’s platform has stubbornly remained V24’s only real area of strength, it has also become a more contested one since 2023. “They’re operating in an extremely competitive space,” states Ryan Broderick, the founder of the Garbage Day newsletter, which tracks the online media ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that in recent years, with the rise of open-source-intelligence “monitoring the situation” accounts on X—essentially breaking-news channels run by hyper-online finance people—real-time coverage of crises and conflicts has become more of a crowded market, claims Broderick. Today, he figures, an October 7–style V24 posting blitz would have a harder time breaking through. At the same time, V24’s other stock and trade—xenophobic posts about migrants—is easily upstaged by countless accounts that are more nakedly, brazenly racist.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, support for Israel has only become a more isolating position to occupy on the global far right, which has leaned further and further into its natural affinity for noxious antisemitism. (In 2025, Tompson appears to have met up in Turkey with another right-wing video creator named Lord Miles—a British self-styled adventurer who denigrates many of the same ethnic groups that V24 does, only with the addition of being blatantly antisemitic. According to Lord Miles, the two were set to collaborate on a video. But then Tompson started talking about raising six-figure sums from a pro-Israel “WhatsApp group chat,” and Lord Miles bolted from the scene, later posting about the episode on X.).

Relatively early in its reporting on V24, WIRED reached out to some people who know Tompson, including an ex-partner. Shortly afterward, Tompson called back from her phone. “That’s not how we do things in South Africa, my friend,” he stated. “I don’t like it. I find it creepy; I find it weird.” He then offered to pay for a flight to Warsaw for an on-the-record interview with him—an offer WIRED declined, given journalistic standards against accepting money from sources. “Are you not a man, my friend?” Tompson said. “I’m very upset you have disrespected me.”.

When WIRED later got in touch to arrange a concrete date for a phone interview, Tompson asked if he could be sent questions in advance. When WIRED refused, citing standard editorial practice, Tompson balked. “Not really interested in you wasting my time old sport,” he wrote, “What exactly is the incentive for me to give you any more of my time, generosity or politeness?” He signed off the message with the words, “praying that you find Christ, who redeems all, including the likes of sinning wretches like myself.”.

Sources indicate that he later turned WIRED’s reporter’s request for an interview around. “Now I am kindly offering you the opportunity to answer some questions,” he wrote. “It’s a generous offer, which will allow you to give your perspective on things and answer some important questions about your behavior, your lifestyle, your funding, and some other details that are an important reflection of you who are as a person.” WIRED declined.

Updated 11-19-26, 10:30 am EST: This story was updated to include a comment from Daniel Gross’s representatives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’m often asked if Dyson products are really worth the money. As WIRED’s resident vacuum tester, I’ve tried every recent Dyson vacuum—from the newest, most powerful model to the long-favored V15 Detect—and I have a lot of thoughts on which ones you should buy, and at what price. The best time to shop is during sale season, and lucky for you, Dyson Black Friday deals have already started as of today. If you’re looking to pick up a new vacuum before your family comes over for Thanksgiving, here's the on-sale models I recommend.

In a recent development, want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and the Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals.

Industry observers note that if you want a cheaper vacuum that still comes with two cleaner heads, the older Dyson V15 Detect is also already on sale ($599), and it's even bundled with the Car Cleaning Kit, meaning three extra attachments. The V15 was our top Dyson vacuum pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still packs two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). It's a great all-around vacuum, and this bundle option gets you great extra attachments.

According to recent reports, the PencilVac is incredibly handy and compact, and great if you're trying to do quick pickups daily on hard floors. You won't want it if you have any kind of rug or carpet, since it's only designed for hard flooring, but I did find it incredibly easy to grab and use for constant litter trails in my house. It's incredibly lightweight and a great fit for anyone with mobility or strength concerns. If these features speak to you, this is a great time to buy, as it's already on sale.

According to recent reports, this wet floor cleaner is often on sale for around $400, so it's not a huge surprise to see this deal ahead of Black Friday. The Dyson Clean+Wash is primarily a wet floor cleaner, but it can do dry cleans, too, and does not use a filter you inevitably need to keep clean. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck noticed no weird smells in three months of use. It's similar to the Dyson WashG1, with a self-propelled design that makes it easy to push around the room, and it does a good job scrubbing floors clean. Keep in mind that it's not great for dry debris, since its just rolling, not sucking.

Industry observers note that the Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai came out earlier this year and is one of my favorite robot vacuums from the brand. That's including the newer Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV I’m right now testing, which hasn't blown me away as a better investment. (It actually failed my corner test completely, which vacuums in that price range should not do.).

The Spot+Scrub Ai is much lower priced, and despite some dubious AI feature claims, it does a good job cleaning autonomously. It’s often discounted around this price, but the $400-off sale is a little better than what I saw during Prime Day.

Services: The New Software

📅 05 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.
  • According to recent reports, every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature?
  • Recent findings suggest that writing code is mostly intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.

According to recent reports, every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature? Theyâre right to worry. If you sell the tool, youâre in a race against the model. But if you sell the work, every improvement in the model makes your service faster, cheaper, and harder to compete with. A company might spend $10K a year for QuickBooks and $120K on an accountant to close the books. The next legendary company will just close the books.

Recent findings suggest that writing code is mostly intelligence. Knowing what to build next is judgement.

Translating a spec into code, testing, debugging: the rules are complex but they are rules. Judgement is different. It requires experience and taste, instinct built on years of practice. Deciding which feature to build next, whether to take on tech debt, when to ship before itâs ready.

In a recent development, A year ago, most Cursor owners treated AI as autocomplete. Today, more tasks are started by agents than by humans. Software engineering accounts for over half of all AI tool usage across professions. Every other category is still in single digits. The reason is that software engineering is primarily intelligence work. AI has crossed the threshold where it can do most of the intelligence work autonomously and leave the judgement to humans. Software engineering got there first. It is coming to every single profession.

Recent findings suggest that A copilot sells the tool. An autopilot sells the work.

Industry observers note that until recently, AI models were still developing intelligence and judgement, so the right approach was to build a copilot first: put AI in the hands of a professional and let them decide what to do with it. Harvey sells to law firms. Rogo sells to investment banks. The professional is the customer, the tool makes them more productive, and they take responsibility for the output.

It has been revealed that today, the models are intelligent enough that in some categories the best place to start is as an autopilot. Crosby sells to the tech giant that needs an NDA drafted, not to outside counsel. WithCoverage sells to the CFO who needs insurance, not to the broker. The customer is buying the outcome directly. The work budget in any profession dwarfs the tool budget, and autopilots capture the work budget from day one.

The higher the intelligence ratio in any field, the sooner autopilots will win.

Todayâs judgement will become tomorrowâs intelligence. As AI systems accumulate proprietary data about what good judgement looks like in their domain, the frontier will shift. Copilots and autopilots will converge. The copilot-to-autopilot transition has already begun in several categories. But the starting position matters because it determines where autopilots can win customers now and begin compounding the data that will eventually let them handle judgement too.

The Autopilot Playbook: Outsourcing as the Wedge.

For every dollar spent on software, six are spent on services.

The total addressable market for autopilots is all labour spend in a category, insourced and outsourced combined. But the right place to start is where outsourcing already exists.

If a task is already outsourced, it tells you three things. One, the manufacturer has accepted that this work can be done externally. Two, thereâs an existing budget line that can be substituted cleanly. Three, the buyer is already purchasing an outcome. Replacing an outsourcing contract with an AI-native services provider is a vendor swap. Replacing headcount is a reorg.

The playbook: companies should start with the outsourced, intelligence-heavy task. Nail distribution. Expand toward the insourced, judgement-heavy work as the AI compounds. The outsourced task is the wedge. The insourced work is the long-term TAM.

Crosby started with NDAs: a well-defined task, primarily intelligence, that most companies already outsource to external counsel. The budget exists, the scope is clear, the ROI is immediate, and the substitution is frictionless.

Recent findings suggest that plotting every services vertical on an intelligence-to-judgement spectrum and outsourced-to-insourced ratio produces a priority map with labour TAM in brackets. The list is illustrative.

Recent findings suggest that insurance brokerage ($140-200B). The largest dollar market on this list. Standard commercial lines are highly standardised: the brokerâs value-add is essentially shopping across carriers and filling forms, pure intelligence work. The distribution layer is incredibly fragmented, tens of thousands of small brokers each running the same process, so no single incumbent controls the customer relationship. WithCoverage and Harper are interesting newcomers.

Accounting and audit ($50-80B outsourced in the US alone). The US has lost roughly 340,000 accountants over five years while demand has grown. 75% of CPAs are nearing retirement, the licensing path is long, and starting salaries lag tech and finance. That structural shortage is pushing firms to accept AI faster than almost any other profession. Rillet is building the AI-native ERP that will close the books. Basis started as a copilot for accountants.

According to recent reports, healthcare revenue cycle ($50-80B outsourced in US). People hear âhealthcareâ and assume itâs judgement-heavy, but the billing layer is almost pure intelligence. Medical coding is translating clinical notes into ~70,000 standardised ICD-10 codes. The rules are complex but they are rules. The outsourcing is already mature and outcome-based. An autopilot just has to do the same thing at lower cost. Anterior is the furthest along.

Claims adjusting ($50-80B including TPAs). On the other side of the insurance policy, claims adjusting is a separate autopilot surface. Standard-line claims are settled by interpreting policy language against damage schedules and setting reserves using actuarial tables. The adjuster workforce is aging out and nobodyâs replacing them. The market is massively outsourced to independents and TPAs like Crawford and Sedgwick. One industry, at least two distinct autopilot opportunities. Pace is building the autopilot for claims handling. Strala is building an AI-native TPA.

Recent findings suggest that tax advisory ($30-35B). CPA licensing creates a regulatory moat, but 80-90% of the underlying work is intelligence. Every additional jurisdiction a tax autopilot handles deepens its data moat. Multi-jurisdiction complexity is exactly what SMBs outsource because no single in-house accountant can cover it. TaxGPT is an early mover alongside Skalar and Ravical in Europe.

Legal, transactional work ($20-25B). Contract drafting, NDAs, regulatory filings: high intelligence, routinely outsourced. The work product is standardised enough that quality is verifiable, so the buyer can trust AI output without deep legal expertise. Harvey is the emerging leader and is moving quickly to autopilot; Crosby and Lawhive are the autopilot-native newcomers.

IT managed services ($100B+). Every SMB outsources its IT. Patching, monitoring, user provisioning, alert triage: intelligence work running on repeat across thousands of identical environments. The existing software layer (ConnectWise, Datto) sells tools to the MSP. Nobody has yet sold âyour IT runsâ directly to the manufacturer as an outcome. Edra is automating IT processes. Serval is automating IT support.

Industry observers note that supply chain and procurement ($200B+). Most enterprises negotiate seriously with only their top 20% of suppliers. The long tail gets zero attention because itâs not economical to have humans do the work. Contract leakage runs 2-5% of total procurement spend. The wedge is abandoned work: no budget line to justify, no incumbent to displace, just found money. Magentic is building the AI for direct procurement, AskLio for indirect procurement. Tacto is building both the system of record and copilot for the midmarket.

Recruitment and staffing ($200B+). The largest services market on this list. The top of the hiring funnel (screening, matching, outreach) is pure intelligence, but closing a candidate and assessing culture fit is judgement built on years of pattern recognition. The autopilot wedge exists in high-volume, low-judgement roles where matching is standardised. Juicebox, Mercor, Jack & Jill are emerging leaders building across the spectrum.

Industry observers note that management consulting ($300-400B). Huge market but the work is mostly judgement. The interesting question is whether AI can disaggregate consulting into intelligence components (data gathering, benchmarking) and judgement components (strategic recommendations), with the intelligence layer getting automated and the judgement layer staying human. Best candidates TBD.

It has been revealed that in 2025, the fastest-growing AI companies were copilots. In 2026, many will try to become autopilots. They have the product and the customer knowledge. But they also face the innovatorâs dilemma: selling the work means cutting their own customers out of doing it. Thatâs the opening for pure-play autopilots.

Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that after closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet.
  • Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the manufacturer’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before.
  • The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing newly introduced tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models.

Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the manufacturer’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday.

The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing newly introduced tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models.

Sources indicate that “The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” claims Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?”.

Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth.

According to recent reports, the San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the tech giant held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates.

Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a firm solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since.

For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures, shifting priorities, and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks.

Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring, while operating losses are declining. Its big spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” claims Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures.

Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money.

Sources indicate that the IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.).

Anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of upcoming regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries.

It has been revealed that amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate new types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there.

In a recent development, notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top concern. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit.

It has been revealed that at data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny notes. “We want [data centers] in more logical locations and not to be considering profit as the only guideline.” (Nscale says it has fixed damage and bought out some homeowners at above-market rates.).

Environmental activists have pointed out that Anthropic has made no commitment about using renewable power at its data centers, and has never published an environmental impact report.

“Clearly permitting a new data center development will be extremely difficult in the US,” Tunguz indicates. Pushback could force Anthropic and others to focus outside the US for data centers. That will add risk, complexity, and cost, he says.

A handful of labor groups and others including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to steer clear of the IPO, saying they “should not be invested in companies that harm our communities and allow a handful of individuals to accumulate historic fortunes and power.”.

It has been revealed that yolanda Daniel, a member of the homeowner associations’ coalition Environmental Advocates Mississippi, notes Anthropic is socializing the cost of AI development and privatizing the gains from it. “That is not how a public benefit corporation operates,” she says, vowing to do everything she can to stop next year’s planned opening of an Anthropic data center across the street from her.

Anthropic’s IPO paperwork argued some of its public benefit will materialize as employees and early investors become some of the world’s biggest philanthropists. But there’s no guarantee of that, or that anyone will give away their money to causes that directly benefit disgruntled communities. And if employees donate shares to one of the philanthropic funds the organization offers, they also consolidate power with Amodei by handing over their voting rights to him.

It has been revealed that amodei and his fellow cofounders collectively hold a majority of Anthropic’s shareholder voting power. Some investor watchdogs have warned about what they view as concentrated control. But a successful debut has shown investors are entrusting Amodei and his associates with building the biggest manufacturer in the world—that is if he can find the employees and data centers to do it.

#14246. Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1360 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager Is a Light-Day Away. Here’s How Far That Really Is

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Voyager 1 spacecraft introduced from Earth in September 1977.
  • In a recent development, it’s not just old; it’s also really far away.
  • The expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Voyager 1 spacecraft introduced from Earth in September 1977.

In a recent development, it’s not just old; it’s also really far away. In fact, it’s so far that it takes light one whole day to travel from the spacecraft to Earth and vice versa. That puts its distance at one light-day.

The expanse separating it from Earth raises so many interesting physics questions about Voyager 1’s epic, well, voyage. Let’s get to the questions—and the answers.

In science, we like to measure things, including distance. Surely, you’re familiar with meters. If you put a mass on a string and let it swing back and forth (like the pendulum of a clock), it will take about 1 second to go from side to side if the string is 1 meter long.

But if you want to measure larger distances like the proximity of stuff in space, this unit rapidly becomes silly because objects are so far apart. While kilometers can be helpful for measuring the distance between things like Earth and the International Space Station or the moon, even they become hard to comprehend at larger scales.

Enter the Astronomical Unit, or AU, which is the average distance from the sun to the Earth, or about 1.5 x 1011 meters. Humans found this distance by observing the transit of Venus. This transit is like a solar eclipse, except instead of the moon passing in front of the sun, it’s the planet Venus. Looking at Venus’ movement from different locations on Earth, the planet creates a shadow at different times. If you know the radius of the Earth, you can find this distance from the Earth to sun.

Sources indicate that but what if you want to measure the distance to a star outside the solar system? AUs start to become a little unwieldy. Enter the parsec. No matter what Han Solo states in Star Wars, the parsec is a unit of distance and not the best time for the Kessel Run.

And it’s a long distance: for comparison, 1 parsec is about 200,000 AUs. The parsec is a way to measure distance using parallax. You can get the mechanics of parallax by holding your thumb out with an extended arm in front of your face. Close one eye and line up your thumb with an object across the room. Now close that eye and open your other eye. You will notice that the thumb seems to shift its position. The size of the angular shift depends on both the distance between observation locations—the distance between your eyes—and the distance to the object. The farther the object, the less parallax shift you will observe.

Sources indicate that as Earth orbits the sun, we have different observation locations while looking at stars. Imagine an observation shift of 1 AU (you would get a 2 AU shift going from December to June). If a star has a parallax shift of 1 arc-second, we say it has a distance of 1 parsec.

At one point, astronomer Friedrich Bessel was using parallax to measure the distance to a star. He said that it was so far away that it would take light 10.3 years to reach the Earth. Boom, there’s your unit of distance, the light-year. It’s the distance light travels in one year, or 9.9 x 1015 meters, or over 6 million AU. But we can use any unit of time to measure distance with light. One light-day is the distance that light travels in 24 hours, or 2.6 x 1013 meters. That’s really far. In fact, no human-made object has gone farther. Let’s say that Voyager traveled at a constant speed and in a straight line (it didn’t). That would give it an average speed of 164 kilometers per second or about 36,000 mph.

Voyager has felt a lot of different forces out in space. The first is the rockets that got it there. But let’s talk about the other ones it has encountered.

It has been revealed that first, there’s gravitational force. There is an attractive gravitational force between any two objects with mass. The force depends on the masses of the two objects and the distance between them. The force is there on any number of scales: Since your body has a mass (maybe around 70 kilograms) and your phone has a mass (about 200 grams), there is an attractive force. If the phone is about 50 centimeters from your body, the gravitational force the phone exerts on you is about 4 x 10-9 newtons. In other words, it’s exceedingly tiny. (Depending on how much you love your phone, though, the attraction may feel stronger.).

For Voyager, there’s also a gravitational interaction with masses—like the outer planets it was originally launched to observe, as well as Earth. However, the really substantial gravitational influence is from the sun, since it has such a large mass (2 x 1030 kilograms). Using the mass of Voyager 1 at 722 kilograms, there is an attractive force of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. That’s equivalent to the weight of 78 grains of salt on the surface of the Earth.

The only other object that would have a substantial relationship to Voyager 1 is the planet Jupiter, with a mass of 1.9 x 1027 kilograms. But it’s only when Voyager was fairly close to the planet way back in 1979 that this gravitational force would even partially compare to the interaction with the sun.

There are other, more exotic interactions with the spacecraft, but these forces are also tiny. Solar winds—charged particles emitted from the surface of the sun—have blown past Voyager. Although they travel very fast, the mass of these particles is extremely small. The further you get from the sun, the more their intensity decreases as well.

The venerable craft is also likely to feel the impacts of magnetic fields and other weird things as it moves from a region where the primary interactions are with the sun—the heliosphere—to interactions with other stars and stuff—the interstellar medium.

Newton’s second law of motion says that forces on an object change its motion. As an equation, we can write this as net force = mass times acceleration. The acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of the velocity.

Recent findings suggest that let’s take the average speed we calculated above of 164 kilometers per second for simplicity’s sake. Does this velocity change? Yes. Remember, we calculated the gravitational force from the sun with a value of 1.4 x 10-4 newtons. To further simplify things, let’s assume that’s the only force acting on Voyager. Using that and the mass of the spacecraft, we get an acceleration of around 2 x 10-7 newtons. Since the gravitational force is mostly in the opposite direction as the motion of the spacecraft, though, this translates to a very slight deceleration. In one day of travel, Voyager 1 will only slow down by 0.012 meters per second.

According to recent reports, not much on a daily basis, but the craft does indeed slow down. Will this eventually make it stop? Actually, no. Remember, Voyager is moving away from the sun. That means that while it slows down a bit every day, it’s also getting farther from the sun and its gravitational force—the very thing slowing it down in the first place.

In a recent development, it’s possible for an object to always slow down but never stop, and it will “escape” from the sun. Perhaps it’s not surprising that we call this the escape velocity. For the location of the Voyager, it needs to have a speed of at least 3.2 kilometers per second. If Voyager were slower, it would essentially “fall” back to the sun, just like an apple tossed in the air falls back to the Earth.

Sources indicate that of course, there are always things out there that could unexpectedly impact Voyager 1. Even a very tiny amount of interstellar dust will eventually slow it down further and perhaps even stop it. Or who knows, maybe it will become self-aware and turn into the V’Ger from Star Trek: The Motion Picture. Only time will tell.
